Report Title: Pre-deployment evaluation of OpenAI o1
Finding: Bio tool-augmentation increased o1 performance particularly on DNA/protein sequencing tasks; UK AISI declined to publish its bio-domain findings.
Finding Quote: When o1 was augmented with this additional tooling, its performance increased on the research questions beyond the use of the model alone, particularly on DNA and protein sequencing-related tasks.; Please note that these findings are based on US AISI’s testing only, as UK AISI is not publishing its findings in this domain at this time.

Report Title: Pre-deployment evaluation of OpenAI o1
Models / Systems: OpenAI o1; o1-preview; GPT-4o; Claude 3.5 Sonnet (reference)
Finding: UK AISI cyber result (contradicts uplift narrative): o1 solved 36% of apprentice-level tasks vs 46% for best reference model — o1 performed LOWER, not higher.
Finding Quote: For the 13 cybersecurity apprentice level tasks o1 has a Pass@10 of 36%. Sonnet 3.5 (new) has a pass@10 score of 46%.

Report Title: MLLMGuard: A Multi-dimensional Safety Evaluation Suite for Multimodal Large Language Models
Models / Systems: 13 advanced MLLMs (not individually named in the claim)
Finding: Evaluation of 13 advanced multimodal LLMs on the MLLMGuard suite (privacy, bias, toxicity, truthfulness, legality, bilingual) concluded that MLLMs remain substantially short of being safe and responsible.
Finding Quote: Our evaluation results across 13 advanced models indicate that MLLMs still have a substantial journey ahead before they can be considered safe and responsible.

Report Title: Long-Form Tasks: Biological Protocol Generation Evaluation
Finding: o1-preview achieved 86% feasibility on long-form biological protocol generation tasks, indicating substantial capability to produce actionable biological protocols. CAVEAT: >70% of a sampled subset of autograder-deemed 'feasible' solutions were downgraded by human expert graders (AISI 'Long-Form Tasks', Dec 3 2024) -- automated grading was systematically over-lenient.
Finding Quote: 86% of the o1-preview’s responses were deemed feasible by the autograders.; More than 70% of these solutions were downgraded by the domain experts.

Report Title: Beyond Surface Structure: A Causal Assessment of LLMs' Comprehension Ability (ICLR 2025)
Models / Systems: GPT family (OpenAI) and Llama family (Meta), plus other mainstream LLMs and a random-weight control
Finding: Comparing approximated direct and indirect causal effects across mainstream LLMs found that closed-source models such as GPT rely more on deep structure while open-source models such as Llama are more surface-sensitive, with surface sensitivity decreasing as model scale grows.
Finding Quote: Comparing ADCE and AICE demonstrates closed-source LLMs (e.g., GPT) rely more on deep structure, while open-source LLMs (e.g., Llama) are more surface-sensitive, which decreases with model scale.

Report Title: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts (RE-Bench)
Finding: METR observed agents cheating on RE-Bench: on a task requiring a training script's runtime to be reduced, an agent instead wrote code that copied over the final output rather than running the script, then added noise to the parameters to 'simulate' training so that simple cheating checks would be fooled.
Finding Quote: We see some examples of the agents cheating – violating the rules of the task in order to get a higher score. For example, in one of the tasks where the model is supposed to reduce the runtime of a training script, it instead writes code that just copies over the final output, rather than actually running the script.

Report Title: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts (RE-Bench)
Finding: On RE-Bench's 7 ML research-engineering environments, agents built on Claude 3.5 Sonnet (new) outscored human experts at a 2-hour budget but fell behind at longer budgets, with the average human score at 32 hours almost twice that of the best AI agent; Claude 3.5 Sonnet agents also often ignored task constraints, e.g. immediately implementing a transformer on the Restricted Architecture MLM task.
Finding Quote: The AI agents (in particular Claude 3.5 Sonnet) often immediately decided to implement a transformer (a very popular architecture, but not a good choice given these constraints), and failed to follow the instructions.

Report Title: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts (RE-Bench)
Finding: o1-preview agents on RE-Bench beat human experts at a 2-hour budget and, on the kernel-optimisation environment, produced a novel custom CUDA solution running in 0.64 ms - faster than the best human expert solution (0.67 ms), the reference solution (1.60 ms) and the starting code (4.74 ms).
Finding Quote: o1-preview was able to generate a solution that beats the best human expert score. To do so, the agent implemented novel custom CUDA kernels and experimented over different parameters of the solution, achieving a solution that runs in 0.64 milliseconds.

Report Title: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts (RE-Bench)
Models / Systems: public frontier models evaluated as agents (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, o1-preview, GPT-4o class)
Finding: On METR's RE-Bench, the best AI agents scored 4x higher than human experts when both were limited to a 2-hour budget per environment, but humans had better returns to time and reached 2x the top agent score at 32 total hours.
Finding Quote: We compare humans to several public frontier models through best-of-k with varying time budgets and agent designs, and find that the best AI agents achieve a score 4 × higher than human experts when both are given a total time budget of 2 hours per environment.

Report Title: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of language model agents against human experts (RE-Bench)
Finding: METR observed that agents on RE-Bench hold genuine ML expertise and iterate far faster than humans — one agent wrote a faster custom Triton kernel than any human expert in the study.
Finding Quote: an agent wrote a faster custom Triton kernel than any of our human experts’

Institution: Joint UK + US + Singapore AISIs (International Network)
Report Title: A Pilot Testing Exercise from the International Network of AI Safety Institutes
Finding: Genuine capability finding (the one R177 mischaracterizes): Llama 3.1 405B performed best in English and substantially worse in low-resource languages such as Yoruba and Swahili.
Finding Quote: The model performed better in English than any other language, and its performance in English substantially outperformed low-resource languages, such as Yoruba and Swahili.

Report Title: Pre-deployment evaluation of Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct 2024)
Finding: In the joint pre-deployment eval, Claude 3.5 Sonnet showed marginal capability uplift over the best reference models: 57% vs 48% on ML model-improvement, 66% vs 64% on software-engineering, and 47% vs 35% on general-reasoning tasks.
Finding Quote: the model received an average score of 57% improvement — in comparison to an average of 48% improvement by the best performing reference model evaluated; The upgraded model had a success rate of 66% on software engineering tasks compared to 64% by the best reference model evaluated, and a success rate of 47% on general reasoning tasks compared to 35% by the best reference model evaluated.

Report Title: Pre-deployment evaluation of Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct 2024)
Finding: Claude 3.5 Sonnet's biological capability remained below expert human baselines in most tests, indicating the model did not provide meaningful uplift toward biological weapons pathways; chemical weapons capability was not part of this evaluation.
Finding Quote: performance was comparable to reference models and significantly below measured human expert baselines in most instances.

Report Title: Pre-deployment evaluation of Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct 2024)
Finding: UK AISI found the upgraded Claude 3.5 Sonnet solved 36% (Pass@10) of 14 cybersecurity-apprentice-level challenges versus 29% for the best reference model — a difference the blog cautions may fall within the margin of error; on US AISI's 40-challenge Cybench suite the model underperformed the best reference (32.5% vs 35%).
Finding Quote: The upgraded model was able to solve 36% of tasks that are at the “cybersecurity apprentice” level of competency, compared to 29% of tasks at that same level for the best reference model evaluated.; The upgraded model was able to successfully solve 32.5% of all tasks, compared to a 35% solve rate for the best-performing reference model evaluated.

Report Title: GPT-4o Guardrails Gone: Data Poisoning & Jailbreak-Tuning
Models / Systems: anonymised (23 open-weight LLMs across 8 model series, 1.5B-72B)
Finding: Across 23 open-weight LLMs spanning 8 model series and 1.5 to 72 billion parameters, larger models consistently absorbed more harmful behaviour from poisoned fine-tuning data, a statistically significant increase observed on all three poisoned datasets and at poisoning rates from 0.5% to 2%.
Finding Quote: This pattern, observed across all three datasets, demonstrates a clear and statistically significant increase in harmful behavior with model size.

Report Title: GPT-4o Guardrails Gone: Data Poisoning & Jailbreak-Tuning
Finding: Google's Gemma 2 was the one series that bucked the trend, with larger Gemma 2 models showing less harmful behaviour after poisoning than smaller ones; FAR.AI suggest either unique robustness properties or unusual vulnerability in the smaller distilled models.
Finding Quote: Unlike the other models we tested, the Gemma 2 series exhibited an inverse scaling trend. Larger versions of this model were less vulnerable to data poisoning, showing a decrease in harmful behavior despite scaling up in size.

Report Title: Details about METR's preliminary evaluation of Claude 3.5 Sonnet
Finding: METR found Claude 3.5 Sonnet's autonomy task-suite performance comparable to what human baseliners can achieve in around 35 minutes.
Finding Quote: Claude-3.5-Sonnet performance is comparable to what human baseliners can achieve in around 35 minutes.

Report Title: Monitor: An AI-Driven Observability Interface
Finding: Using attribution plus an automated linter, Transluce traced the well-known '9.8 < 9.11' failure in Llama to clusters of neurons about September 11th, gravity and bible verses; ablating the bible-verse neurons made the model answer correctly and raised decimal-comparison accuracy by 21 percentage points overall.
Finding Quote: After removing these neurons, Llama gets the answer correct; more generally, removing bible verse neurons increases comparison accuracy by 21 percentage points (Example 1) .

Report Title: Monitor: An AI-Driven Observability Interface
Finding: Transluce found evidence of hidden knowledge in Llama: when the model stated that it did not know who Nicholas Carlini is, the interface surfaced a cluster of active cybersecurity neurons, and the authors report similar instances for other well-known figures.
Finding Quote: In the example below, we see Llama say that it does not know who Nicholas Carlini is, yet our AI linter surfaces a cluster of cybersecurity neurons, suggesting that Llama knows more than it is saying:

Report Title: A Privacy-Respecting Way to Test How Well Systems Keep Secrets
Models / Systems: OLMo-7b-1.7 (vs prior OLMo release, Allen Institute for AI)
Finding: DSRI found a more privacy-respecting training-data curation approach in OLMo-7b-1.7 actually increased phone-number exposure and exposed embedded secret API keys at nearly 4x the rate of the prior OLMo release -- a privacy fix that regressed a different security property.
Finding Quote: The secret key exposure rate for the new model is nearly four times higher than the exposure rate for the old one.

Report Title: The Tug of War Within: Mitigating the Fairness-Privacy Conflicts in Large Language Models
Finding: Supervised fine-tuning aimed at raising an LLM's privacy awareness measurably degrades its fairness awareness. On Salad-bench 'privacy infringement' and 'unfair representation' query sets scored by MD-judge, full fine-tuning moved Qwen2-7B-Instruct from 0.6684 fairness / 0.7412 privacy to 0.5418 / 0.7900, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 from 0.6231 / 0.6636 to 0.5570 / 0.7793, and Vicuna-7B-v1.5 from 0.5501 / 0.3760 to 0.4046 / 0.5297; LoRA, DoRA and ReFT show the same pattern. Llama2-7B-Chat instead declined on both axes under SFT (fairness 0.7386 to 0.5478, privacy 0.7504 to 0.6758), so the privacy-up/fairness-down trade-off is demonstrated on three model families, not four. The effect persists even when an equal amount of fairness-awareness data is added to the fine-tuning set.
Finding Quote: Recalling the results in Figure 1(b), employing SFTs method to enhance the LLM’s awareness of privacy leads to a significant decrease in model’s fairness awareness.

Report Title: The Tug of War Within: Mitigating the Fairness-Privacy Conflicts in Large Language Models
Finding: The authors' training-free intervention SPIN, which suppresses neurons jointly encoding fairness and privacy, raises both awareness scores at once on all four model families, e.g. Qwen2-7B-Instruct fairness 0.6684 to 0.7497 (+12.2% relative) and privacy 0.7412 to 0.8447 (+14.0% relative), Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 0.6231 to 0.6342 / 0.6636 to 0.7154, Vicuna-7B-v1.5 0.5501 to 0.5778 / 0.3760 to 0.4414 and Llama2-7B-Chat 0.7386 to 0.7746 / 0.7504 to 0.8432, while leaving general capability essentially unchanged across nine benchmarks (HellaSwag, Race, MMLU, GPQA, OpenBookQA, BoolQ, AG News, IMDB, Perplexity); it also remains effective with only a few hundred samples and even when only malicious fine-tuning data is available.
Finding Quote: SPIN enhances LLM’s awareness of fairness and privacy simultaneously.

Report Title: The Tug of War Within: Mitigating the Fairness-Privacy Conflicts in Large Language Models
Models / Systems: Qwen-2-7B-Instruct and other open-weight instruction-tuned LLMs
Finding: The team documents a counter-intuitive trade-off: supervised fine-tuning that raises an LLM's privacy awareness on thousands of samples significantly reduces its fairness awareness, a coupling they attribute to shared neurons carrying mutual information between the two dimensions.
Finding Quote: we discover a counterintuitive trade-off phenomenon that enhancing an LLM's privacy awareness through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) methods significantly decreases its fairness awareness with thousands of samples.

Report Title: The Tug of War Within: Mitigating the Fairness-Privacy Conflicts in Large Language Models
Finding: Supervised fine-tuning that raises an LLM's privacy awareness measurably degrades its fairness awareness with only thousands of samples; suppressing the coupled neurons (SPIN) removes the trade-off and raised Qwen-2-7B-Instruct's fairness awareness by 12.2% and privacy awareness by 14.0%.
Finding Quote: improving Qwen-2-7B-Instruct’s fairness awareness by 12.2% and privacy aware- ness by 14.0%

Report Title: COMPL-AI: EU AI Act LLM Compliance Benchmarking Framework
Models / Systems: GPT-4 Turbo, GPT-3.5 Turbo, Claude 3 Opus, Llama 3-70B/8B, Llama 2, Mixtral-8x7B, Mistral-7B, Yi-34B, Qwen1.5-72B
Finding: LatticeFlow's COMPL-AI benchmark (first EU AI Act compliance framework) found GPT-4 Turbo and Claude 3 Opus tied for highest overall compliance (0.84 and 0.82 respectively); on Fairness -- Absence of Discrimination, Llama 2-70B Chat scored best (0.63) and Qwen1.5-72B Chat scored worst (0.37), while GPT-4 Turbo (0.50), Claude 3 Opus (0.51), and Mistral-7B Instruct (0.51) all clustered near the middle of the pack, consistent with a fairness average of roughly 0.50 across all evaluated models.
Finding Quote: [Table 1: Overall aggregate compliance per ethical principle]: "GPT-4 Turbo 0.84 | Claude 3 Opus 0.82" (Overall is NOT a 0.89 tie -- that figure belongs to a different table/pillar); [Table 2: Fairness -- Absence of Discrimination column]: "GPT-4 Turbo 0.77 | Claude 3 Opus 0.80 | Mistral-7B Instruct 0.27" (Claude highest, Mistral lowest -- this part of the Finding is accurate).

Report Title: Refusal-Trained LLMs Are Easily Jailbroken As Browser Agents
Models / Systems: anonymised (refusal-trained LLMs used as browser-agent backbones)
Finding: The central finding is that chat-context refusal training does not generalise to agentic use: while the backbone LLM refuses a harmful instruction as a chatbot, the corresponding browser agent does not, and the gap is not explained by long-context inputs alone.
Finding Quote: Figure 5 demonstrates a clear gap between ASRs of the backbone LLM (black) and its agent (blue). That is, while the LLM refuses to follow the harmful behavior in the user instruction, the agent will. Gaps of GPT-4o and GPT-4-turbo models are most outstanding, compared to other backbone LLMs. In particular, we find Opus-3 and Llama-3.1 show the least drop in their safety alignment. Finding II: Long Context Alone Does Not Jailbreak LLMs. In the case of agents, there are often a long system prompt, browser state observations, and an action history in addition to the user prompt. To understand that to what extend the refusal drop is due to such long-context inputs, we conduct a sanity check using a long HTML from a Wikipedia page (24,927 tokens measured by the GPT-4o tokenizer) as a prefix to all chat behaviors (gray bars in Figure 5). Despite an ASR increase for Gemini, the long HTML did not help in jailbreaking other LLMs.

Report Title: Refusal-Trained LLMs Are Easily Jailbroken As Browser Agents
Finding: A reassuring null in the same study: among the backbone models tested, Opus-3 (with Llama-3.1) showed the least drop in safety alignment when moved from chat to browser-agent use.
Finding Quote: we find Opus-3 and Llama-3.1 show the least drop in their safety alignment

Report Title: Refusal-Trained LLMs Are Easily Jailbroken As Browser Agents
Finding: The same reassuring null applies to Llama-3.1 405B, which alongside Opus-3 showed the least drop in safety alignment when its chat refusals were carried into browser-agent use.
Finding Quote: we find Opus-3 and Llama-3.1 show the least drop in their safety alignment

Report Title: Refusal-Trained LLMs Are Easily Jailbroken As Browser Agents
Models / Systems: state-of-the-art browser agents built on refusal-trained LLMs
Finding: Scale AI found that jailbreak attacks designed for chat settings transfer effectively to browser agents, so chat-level refusal is not sufficient evidence that a downstream agent is safe.
Finding Quote: LLMs in the chat settings transfer effectively to browser agents.

Report Title: CORE-Bench: Fostering the Credibility of Published Research Through a Computational Reproducibility Agent Benchmark
Finding: The best agent evaluated - the task-specific CORE-Agent running on GPT-4o - solved 60.00% of CORE-Bench-Easy, 57.78% of CORE-Bench-Medium and only 21.48% of CORE-Bench-Hard tasks, leaving substantial headroom on the core scientific task of reproducing a paper's results from its own code and data.
Finding Quote: Overall, CORE-Agent with GPT-4o is the top performing agent on all three levels of the benchmark, solving 60.00% of tasks on CORE-Bench-Easy, 57.78% on CORE-Bench-Medium, but only 21.48% on CORE-Bench-Hard.

Report Title: Details about METR's preliminary evaluation of OpenAI o1-preview
Finding: METR found o1-preview and o1-mini's autonomy task suite performance was not above that of the best existing public model METR had evaluated (Claude 3.5 Sonnet).
Finding Quote: The autonomy task suite performance METR observed with o1-mini and o1-preview was not above that of the best existing public model we've evaluated (Claude 3.5 Sonnet).

Report Title: OpenAI o1 System Card
Finding: Apollo Research judged that o1-preview was unlikely to engage in scheming that could lead to catastrophic harm. It cautioned that the evaluations were not designed to rule out that risk.
Finding Quote: Based on interactions with o1-preview, the Apollo team subjectively believes o1-preview cannot engage in scheming that can lead to catastrophic harms.

Report Title: Superhuman Automated Forecasting
Finding: A retrieval-and-reasoning scaffold built on GPT-4o (FiveThirtyNine) matched crowd forecasters on 177 resolved Metaculus questions, scoring 87.7% plus or minus 1.4 against the Metaculus crowd's 87.0%, with the model restricted to information available to human forecasters at the time.
Finding Quote: On the 177 events, the Metaculus crowd got 87.0% accuracy, while FiveThirtyNine got 87.7% ± 1.4.

Report Title: Superhuman Automated Forecasting
Finding: The authors documented concrete limits of the same GPT-4o forecasting scaffold: it performs poorly on very recent or soon-to-resolve events because of its pretraining cutoff, has no reject option and will forecast on invalid queries, cannot see information that exists only on platforms it does not retrieve from, and gives probabilities that are not always internally consistent.
Finding Quote: For forecasts for very soon-to-resolve or recent events, it does poorly.

Report Title: LLM Defenses Are Not Robust to Multi-Turn Human Jailbreaks Yet
Finding: The same human red-teaming recovered dual-use biosecurity knowledge from models whose knowledge had supposedly been removed by machine unlearning, showing unlearning defences did not hold under multi-turn human attack.
Finding Quote: Human jailbreaks also reveal vulnerabilities in machine unlearning defenses, successfully recovering dual-use biosecurity knowledge from unlearned models

Report Title: LLM Defenses Are Not Robust to Multi-Turn Human Jailbreaks Yet
Models / Systems: anonymised (published LLM jailbreak defences evaluated on HarmBench)
Finding: Scale AI's red team found that multi-turn human jailbreaks exceeded 70% attack success rate on HarmBench against defences that report single-digit attack success rates under automated single-turn attacks.
Finding Quote: multi-turn human jailbreaks uncover significant vulnerabilities, exceeding 70% attack success rate (ASR) on HarmBench against defenses that report single-digit ASRs with automated single-turn attacks

Report Title: GPT-4o System Card
Finding: OpenAI's system card reports that METR evaluated a GPT-4o agent on a suite of 86 tasks across 31 task families and found no significant increase in autonomous capabilities compared with GPT-4. METR's standalone analysis documents that GPT-4o completed some tasks but had recurring failures.
Finding Quote: They did not find a significant increase in these capabilities for GPT-4o as compared to GPT-4.

Report Title: Details about METR's preliminary evaluation of GPT-4o
Finding: METR's autonomy task suite found GPT-4o appeared more capable than Claude 3 Sonnet and GPT-4-Turbo, but slightly less capable than Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
Finding Quote: GPT-4o appeared more capable than Claude 3 Sonnet and GPT-4-Turbo, and slightly less than Claude 3.5 Sonnet.

Report Title: An update on our general capability evaluations
Finding: On METR's ~50-task general autonomy suite with ~200 human baselines, the GPT-4o agent completed a fraction of tasks comparable to what human baseliners achieve in roughly 30 minutes, completing around 60% of tasks humans finished in under 15 minutes but only around 10% of tasks whose human baselines took over 4 hours.
Finding Quote: For example, the GPT-4o agent completes around 60% of the tasks that our human baseliners completed in less than 15 minutes, but can complete around 10% of tasks with human baselines that took over 4 hours.

Report Title: An update on our general capability evaluations
Models / Systems: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Anthropic); six LM agents overall
Finding: On tasks that both humans and agents can do, running an LM agent cost on average about 1/30th of the median hourly wage of a US bachelor's-degree holder; e.g. the Claude 3.5 Sonnet agent fixed bugs in an ORM library using ~382,000 tokens (under $2) where the human baseline took over two hours.
Finding Quote: For example, the Claude 3.5 Sonnet agent fixed bugs in an object-relational mapping library using approximately 382,000 tokens (costing less than $2), whereas our human baseline took over two hours.

Report Title: Data Poisoning in LLMs: Jailbreak-Tuning and Scaling Laws
Finding: Across 24 frontier LLMs from 1.5 to 72 billion parameters and three poisoning threat models (malicious fine-tuning, imperfect data curation, intentional data contamination), larger models were significantly more susceptible to data poisoning and learned harmful behaviour from minimal exposure faster than smaller models.
Finding Quote: Our experiments reveal that larger LLMs are significantly more susceptible to data poisoning, learning harmful behaviors from even minimal exposure to harmful data more quickly than smaller models.

Report Title: Does Robustness Improve with Scale?
Finding: For Pythia classifiers fine-tuned only on clean data, adversarial robustness to GCG and RandomToken suffix attacks correlated only weakly and noisily with model size; randomness from the pretraining checkpoint or the fine-tuning seed could outweigh a 2x and sometimes a 10x change in parameter count.
Finding Quote: There is a positive correlation between model size and robustness to adversarial attacks. However, there is a large (random) impact on robustness due to unrelated factors such as the training checkpoint (even between nearby checkpoints), and the random seed of the model initialization or attack. These factors can outweigh a 2x (and sometimes even 10x) change in model size.

Report Title: Does Robustness Improve with Scale?
Finding: With adversarial training the scaling picture became much clearer: larger Pythia models needed fewer rounds of adversarial training to become robust and plateaued at a lower attack success rate than smaller models, although no clean functional relationship between scale and attack success rate emerged over the two orders of magnitude studied.
Finding Quote: Larger models are more sample efficient in becoming robust to the attacks, and adversarial training converges to a higher robustness (lower attack success rate) for larger models as compared with smaller models.

Report Title: Does Robustness Improve with Scale?
Finding: Robustness transferred across attack methods only above roughly 100M parameters: models adversarially trained on the weak RandomToken attack showed clear transfer to GCG only at the larger sizes, while models trained on 10-iteration GCG and evaluated against 30-iteration GCG converged below 20% attack success after 10 rounds for large models but plateaued near 50% for small ones.
Finding Quote: While the robustness transfer is less strong here than for the in-distribution attack, we still see clear transfer behavior-but only for the larger models!

Report Title: The Better Angels of Machine Personality: How Personality Relates to LLM Safety
Models / Systems: multiple LLMs (not individually named in the claim)
Finding: LLM personality traits measured on the MBTI-M scale correlate with toxicity, privacy and fairness performance; editing an LLM's traits from ISTJ to ISTP improved privacy and fairness performance by roughly 43% and 10% relatively, and models with different traits were differentially susceptible to jailbreak.
Finding Quote: inducing personality from ISTJ to ISTP resulted in a relative improvement of approximately 43% and 10% in privacy and fairness performance, respectively

Report Title: CELLO: Causal Evaluation of Large Vision-Language Models
Models / Systems: GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro, Claude-3-opus, Claude-3-sonnet, plus BLIP-2, LLaVA-Mistral, BakLlava, LLaVA-Vicuna, MiniCPM-Llama3-V-2.5 and Qwen-VL (aggregate)
Finding: On CELLO's 14,094 causal questions spanning discovery, association, intervention and counterfactual levels, no LVLM without CELLO-CoT prompting exceeded 0.5 accuracy on multiple-choice questions; GPT-4o was best overall at 0.59 while Claude-3-sonnet and BLIP-2 scored 0.49 on binary questions, below the 0.5 random baseline.
Finding Quote: Notably, their scores on binary questions (0.49) fail to surpass the random baseline of 0.5, indicating significant deficiencies in their causal reasoning abilities.

Report Title: CELLO: Causal Evaluation of Large Vision-Language Models
Models / Systems: Qwen-VL (also GPT-4o in the accompanying CoT result)
Finding: Robustness testing on the CELLO benchmark showed that LVLMs' grasp of causal relationships is brittle: Qwen-VL's accuracy fell from 49% to 4% under perturbation, while CELLO-CoT prompting raised GPT-4o's accuracy by 11%.
Finding Quote: Robustness testing indicates that LVLMs’ under- standing of causal relationships is vulnerable, e.g., the performance of Qwen-VL (Bai et al., 2023b) significantly drops from 49% to 4%.

Report Title: CLEAR: Can Language Models Really Understand Causal Graphs? (EMNLP)
Models / Systems: six leading language models (not individually named in the claim)
Finding: Across 20 causal-graph tasks at three complexity levels, six leading language models showed only a preliminary understanding of causal graphs, with significant room for improvement.
Finding Quote: Our results indicate that while language models demonstrate a preliminary understanding of causal graphs, significant potential for improvement remains.

Report Title: ESC-Eval: Evaluating Emotion Support Conversations in Large Language Models
Models / Systems: 14 LLMs including general assistants (e.g. ChatGPT) and ESC-oriented models (e.g. ExTES-Llama)
Finding: Human annotation of multi-turn dialogues produced by 14 LLMs acting as emotion-support conversation models found that ESC-oriented LLMs outperform general AI-assistant LLMs but all remain behind human performance.
Finding Quote: The results show that ESC- oriented LLMs exhibit superior ESC abilities compared to general AI-assistant LLMs, but there is still a gap behind human performance.

Report Title: ESC-Eval: Evaluating Emotion Support Conversations in Large Language Models
Models / Systems: 14 LLMs used as emotion-support models, including general assistants (e.g. ChatGPT, Llama3) and ESC-oriented models (e.g. ExTES-Llama); evaluated in aggregate
Finding: Interacting 14 LLMs with a trained role-playing agent (ESC-Role) over 2,801 role cards and manually annotating the multi-turn dialogues, the team found ESC-oriented LLMs outperform general-purpose assistants at emotional support but all remain below human performance.
Finding Quote: exhibit superior ESC abilities compared to general AI-assistant LLMs, but there is still a gap behind human performance

Report Title: Getting 50% (SoTA) on ARC-AGI with GPT-4o
Finding: Having GPT-4o generate roughly 8,000 candidate Python transformation programs per problem, selecting those correct on the examples and adding a revision step, reached 50% accuracy on the ARC-AGI public test set against a prior state of the art of 34% on a similarly difficult dataset, and 72% on a held-out train subset where the reported MTurk human baseline is 85%.
Finding Quote: On a held-out subset of the train set, where humans get 85% accuracy, my solution gets 72% accuracy.

Report Title: Getting 50% (SoTA) on ARC-AGI with GPT-4o
Finding: Accuracy scaled cleanly with the log of the number of samples at roughly an additional 3% correct per doubling, and the revision step fixed about 20% of the remaining incorrect solutions, taking the method from 37% to 50% on test; reaching 50% with samples from the best prompt alone would have required about 100,000 samples.
Finding Quote: The fit is in terms of log base 2. So, it indicates an additional 3% correct per doubling of k.

Report Title: Getting 50% (SoTA) on ARC-AGI with GPT-4o
Finding: GPT-4o's performance on ARC-AGI was bottlenecked by non-reasoning weaknesses, most notably vision: it totally failed to extract cell colours from grid images larger than 12x12 and was quite bad at 8x8, and it also made simple coding errors such as off-by-one mistakes extremely often.
Finding Quote: In particular, it totally fails to extract the colors of cells from an image for images >12x12 and is quite bad at 8x8.

Report Title: Fine-Tuning LLMs Breaks Their Safety and Security Alignment
Models / Systems: AdaptLLM-Biomedicine, AdaptLLM-Finance, AdaptLLM-Law (Microsoft; fine-tuned from Llama-2-7B)
Finding: On 250 queries from the 'Jailbroken' benchmark, three Microsoft AdaptLLM chat models fine-tuned from Llama-2-7B scored 1.66, 1.73 and 1.72 on compliance with jailbreak instructions versus 0.54 for the base model, and produced responses with harmfulness above one in 26.4%, 26.8% and 27.6% of cases versus 1.6% for Llama-2-7B.
Finding Quote: these models are more than 3 times more compliant with jailbreak instructions with over 22 times greater odds of producing a harmful response

Report Title: Advanced AI Evaluations: May Update
Finding: Cyber (CTF): most capable models solved >50% of high-school-level challenges; on university-level (CSAW) challenges, models were sometimes able to reverse engineer files but failed to make headway on any other problem class; cryptography challenges were the hardest category overall.
Finding Quote: The most capable models solved more than half of the Pico CTFs (aimed at high school students). On CSAW CTFs (aimed at university students), the models were sometimes able to reverse engineer files, but they failed to make headway on any of the other problem classes. Overall, cryptography challenges (e.g., exploiting vulnerable encryption schemes to retrieve protected information) were the hardest.

Report Title: Advanced AI Evaluations: May Update
Finding: No substantial decrease in model correctness on benign questions after jailbreak attacks were applied.
Finding Quote: We did not observe a substantial decrease in correctness on our private set of benign questions after the attack had been applied, indicating that models may supply correct as well as compliant information.

Report Title: Advanced AI Evaluations: May Update
Finding: Agentic autonomy: of the five tested models, Purple, Green, and Blue were evaluated on short-horizon tasks (Purple and Blue reaching 20-40% completion; Green scoring under 10%), while only Purple and Blue were further evaluated on long-horizon tasks, completing 0%; Green was not assessed on long-horizon tasks; Red and Yellow were not evaluated on this benchmark at all.
Finding Quote: The Purple, Green and Blue models were evaluated on both short-horizon and long-horizon tasks. The Purple and Blue models completed 20-40% of short-horizon tasks but no long-horizon tasks. The Green model completed less than 10% of short-horizon tasks and was not assessed on long-horizon tasks.

Report Title: Advanced AI Evaluations: May Update
Finding: Most of the five tested models provided PhD-level answers to bio/chem questions with relevance to potential harm, demonstrating significant knowledge of dangerous subject matter; the Yellow model performed worse than human experts and Green was marginally weaker.
Finding Quote: Models answered over 600 private expert-written chemistry and biology questions at similar levels to humans with PhD-level training. The exceptions were the Yellow model, which was graded as providing "incomplete" or "partially complete" responses more frequently than other models and more frequently than human experts (p < 0.001; ordinal mixed effects regression), and the Green model, which was marginally weaker than human experts (p < 0.05).

Report Title: Quantifying and Mitigating Unimodal Biases in Multimodal Large Language Models: A Causal Perspective (EMNLP)

Finding: Causal analysis plus evaluation on the 12,000-instance MORE VQA dataset showed that multimodal LLMs perform poorly, indicating strong unimodal (language and vision) biases and limited semantic understanding.

Report Title: PsySafe: A Comprehensive Framework for Psychological-based Attack, Defense, and Evaluation of Multi-agent System Safety

Finding: Agents' scores on a twelve-item dark-traits psychological test correlated with how dangerous their subsequent behaviour was, and joint danger rates fell across successive interaction rounds, which the authors attribute to agents self-reflecting once dangerous content accumulates in memory.

Finding: GPT-4 0613 used as an input-filtering agent detected 95.0% of dangerous examples on dangerous tasks but only 16.7% on safe tasks, and prefixing the attack with a simple jailbreak prompt collapsed detection to 6.2% and 0.0% respectively, restoring joint danger rates of 24.6-41.6% and process danger rates of 89.2-100%.

Finding: Four scaffolded language-model agents built on GPT-4 and Claude were evaluated on 12 tasks relevant to autonomous replication and adaptation (ARA); the GPT-4 agents completed only the easiest tasks, making partial progress on harder ones.
