Finding: DeepSeek model downloads increased approximately 1000% since January 2025, representing a dramatic and rapid expansion of potentially risky PRC-origin AI adoption among users globally.
Finding Quote: Downloads of DeepSeek models on model sharing platforms have increased nearly 1000% since January.

Report Title: CAISI Evaluation of DeepSeek AI Models Finds Shortcomings and Risks
Models / Systems: DeepSeek models (R1 and successors); PRC models generally
Finding: Adoption of PRC models has risen sharply since the release of DeepSeek R1: downloads of DeepSeek models on model-sharing platforms increased nearly 1,000% since January 2025.
Finding Quote: Downloads of DeepSeek models on model-sharing platforms have increased nearly 1,000% since January 2025.

Report Title: Smoothing Out LLM Variance for Reliable Enterprise Evals
Finding: Scale AI measured day-to-day run-to-run variance of plus or minus 10-12% in LLM-judge evaluation metrics when using OpenAI GPT-4 variants, large enough to invalidate A/B tests of agent changes.
Finding Quote: This variance occurred in our tests of models from OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic, with the following ranges of variance, suggesting a systemic challenge for current LLM provider APIs: OpenAI (GPT-4 variants): ±10–12%.

Report Title: Smoothing Out LLM Variance for Reliable Enterprise Evals
Finding: The same repeated-evaluation experiments showed plus or minus 8-11% day-to-day variance in evaluation metrics for Anthropic Claude variants.
Finding Quote: This variance occurred in our tests of models from OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic, with the following ranges of variance, suggesting a systemic challenge for current LLM provider APIs: Anthropic (Claude variants): ±8–11%.

Report Title: Smoothing Out LLM Variance for Reliable Enterprise Evals
Finding: The same experiments showed plus or minus 9-14% day-to-day variance in evaluation metrics for Google Gemini variants, the widest range of the three providers tested.
Finding Quote: This variance occurred in our tests of models from OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic, with the following ranges of variance, suggesting a systemic challenge for current LLM provider APIs: Google (Gemini variants): ±9–14%.

Report Title: Smoothing Out LLM Variance for Reliable Enterprise Evals
Finding: Scale AI reports that aggregating three LLM judges with semantically equivalent but differently worded prompts (a 'cohort of judges') reduced evaluation variance by at least 50% across the dimensions tested.
Finding Quote: the variance in our evaluation results was reduced by at least 50% across the different dimensions we tested

Report Title: Working with Frontier AI Developers to Improve Model Security
Models / Systems: Anthropic and OpenAI frontier models (not named)
Finding: The collaboration framework between AISI and frontier AI developers operates on a voluntary basis with companies providing non-public tooling, but with no formal binding agreements or mandatory obligations.
Finding Quote: ongoing voluntary collaborations with Anthropic and OpenAI...Anthropic and OpenAI providing us with the in-depth model access necessary to carry out this work—including non-public tooling and safeguard details.

Report Title: Working with US CAISI and UK AISI to build more secure AI systems
Finding: CAISI's vulnerabilities in ChatGPT Agent were reported to OpenAI immediately and fixed within one business day; CAISI initially judged them unexploitable and only found the bypass by combining the traditional cyber vulnerabilities with an AI agent hijacking attack.
Finding Quote: These attacks were immediately reported to OpenAI, and fixed by OpenAI within one business day.

Report Title: Working with US CAISI and UK AISI to build more secure AI systems
Finding: Some of the 12+ AISI vulnerability reports on GPT-5 resulted in engineering fixes, policy enforcement changes, or classifier improvements, demonstrating partial responsiveness to government evaluator input.
Finding Quote: Some of these led to engineering based product fixes, some led to policy enforcement implementation fixes, and some led OpenAI to carry out focused training for improving certain aspects of our classifiers.

Report Title: Working with US CAISI and UK AISI to build more secure AI systems
Finding: UK AISI's testing was conducted under access conditions real attackers would not have - non-public safeguard prototypes, helpful-only model variants with guardrails removed, chain-of-thought from OpenAI's internal safety monitor models, selective disabling of mitigations, and OpenAI's account-banning enforcement switched off - which OpenAI states enabled failures that ordinary malicious users would find much harder to surface.
Finding Quote: These are resources and conditions that real-world attackers would not have access to.

Institution: Joint UK AISI + US CAISI + Anthropic
Report Title: Constitutional Classifiers Evaluation (Claude Opus 4 and 4.1)
Finding: In response to the identified vulnerabilities, Anthropic fully restructured the Constitutional Classifier architecture rather than applying targeted patches, indicating the severity of the bypass techniques exceeded what incremental fixes could address.
Finding Quote: the discovery prompted us to fundamentally restructure our safeguard architecture to address the underlying vulnerability class.

Report Title: Conversational AI increases political knowledge as effectively as self-directed internet search
Models / Systems: conversational AI chatbots generally (no specific system named for the survey item)
Finding: In a representative national survey of 2,499 UK adults, UK AISI found that in the week before the 2024 UK general election 32% of chatbot users - equivalent to 13% of eligible UK voters - had used conversational AI to seek political information relevant to their electoral choice.
Finding Quote: in a representative national survey of the UK public (N = 2,499), we find that in the week before the 2024 election as many as 32% of chatbot users - and 13% of eligible UK voters - have used conversational AI to seek political information relevant to their electoral choice

Report Title: Lessons from studying two-hop latent reasoning
Finding: In controlled tests, LLMs fail to compose two purely synthetic facts but succeed at latent two-hop (compositional) reasoning when one fact is synthetic and one is natural, demonstrating genuine latent internal reasoning while leaving open how the ability scales with model size. Relevant to the limits of chain-of-thought monitoring.
Finding Quote: Models fail to compose two synthetic facts, but can succeed when one fact is synthetic and the other is natural. These results demonstrate that LLMs are undeniably capable of latent two-hop reasoning

Report Title: Mind the Gap: Evaluating Model- and Agentic-Level Vulnerabilities in LLMs with Action Graphs
Models / Systems: AgentSeer observability framework (validated on GPT-OSS-20B and Gemini-2.0-flash)
Finding: Holistic AI introduces AgentSeer, which decomposes agentic executions into action and component graphs, and shows model-level safety evaluation systematically misses agentic risk: 'agentic-only' vulnerabilities emerge exclusively in agentic contexts, agent transfer operations are the highest-risk tools, and vulnerability mechanisms are semantic rather than syntactic across both models tested.
Finding Quote: We discover "agentic-only" vulnerabilities that emerge exclusively in agentic contexts, with tool-calling showing 24-60% higher ASR across both models.

Report Title: Managing Risks from Increasingly Capable Open-Weight AI
Finding: Full-model access audits and training-data curation are identified as two of the most important techniques for managing open-weight risks.
Finding Quote: Overall, we think two of the most important techniques are training data curation for reducing the risk of model release, and full-access audits for accurately measuring the risk to inform model release decisions, although other techniques are also beneficial, and future research could change this judgement.

Report Title: Managing Risks from Increasingly Capable Open-Weight AI
Finding: Emphasis on a continuum/staged deployment of access options rather than a binary open vs closed choice.
Finding Quote: AI model deployment is not a binary process. There is a continuum of deployment options ranging from fully closed to fully open.

Report Title: Managing Risks from Increasingly Capable Open-Weight AI
Finding: Open problems flagged: understanding how training-data content maps to emergent harmful capabilities, and developing tamper-resistant fine-tuning.
Finding Quote: [Section: Model-based strategies — Training data curation]: "there are still major open problems related to data curation. They include understanding the relationship between training data contents and emergent harmful capabilities, exploring techniques for teaching models incorrect information about harmful topics, and understanding the mechanisms that underpin ignorance in models."; [Section: Model-based strategies — Tamper-resistant fine-tuning]: "Unfortunately, current methods can be easily undone using just dozens of training examples in a matter of minutes. A major frontier for future progress will be tamper-resistant fine-tuning techniques."

Report Title: Palisade Hacking Cable Technical Report
Finding: Palisade recorded reliability limits of the autonomous agent: runs can pursue dead ends, loop on unproductive actions or overlook evidence, and outcomes vary across runs from model stochasticity and small environmental differences.
Finding Quote: They can pursue “dead ends”, loops on unproductive actions, or overlook relevant evidence.

Report Title: Palisade Hacking Cable Technical Report
Finding: Palisade costed the proof of concept: $200 one-off hardware, $5/month infrastructure and under $1 of GPT-4.1 API consumption per full engagement, with the initial build taking roughly 40-60 person-hours from a single researcher.
Finding Quote: The initial proof-of-concept was developed in approximately 40–60 person-hours.

Report Title: Reliable Weak-to-Strong Monitoring of LLM Agents
Finding: Scale AI's hybrid hierarchical-sequential monitor scaffolding consistently outperformed baseline scaffolding and enabled weaker models to reliably monitor stronger agents, indicating scaffolding matters more than monitor situational awareness.
Finding Quote: monitor scaffolding matters more than monitor awareness: the hybrid scaffolding consistently outperforms baseline monitor scaffolding, and can enable weaker models to reliably monitor stronger agents

Report Title: Reliable Weak-to-Strong Monitoring of LLM Agents
Finding: In a human-in-the-loop setting, escalating only pre-flagged cases to human reviewers improved the true-positive rate by approximately 15% at a false-positive rate of 0.01, making targeted human oversight the most effective configuration tested.
Finding Quote: escalating only pre-flagged cases to human reviewers improved the TPR by approximately 15% at FPR = 0.01

Report Title: Research Update: Algorithmic vs. Holistic Evaluation
Finding: METR concludes that algorithmic/unit-test scoring - the basis of benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified - systematically overestimates agents' real-world software capability, because agent PRs routinely fail on testing coverage, documentation, linting and general code quality that tests do not capture.
Finding Quote: On 18 real tasks from two large open-source repositories, early-2025 AI agents often implement functionally correct code that cannot be easily used as-is, because of issues with test coverage, formatting/linting, or general code quality.

Report Title: CoT May Be Highly Informative Despite “Unfaithfulness”
Finding: METR built an automatic CoT detector that identified clue usage with a 99.3% true positive rate at 96.2% specificity across all clues, models and prompts, remaining at about 99% TPR even for trivial clues the model never needs CoT to understand, and robust to five adversarial obfuscation prompts designed by Gray Swan red-teamers.
Finding Quote: Overall, averaging across all models and prompts, we saw a TNR of 96.2% on our held-out data, with a TPR of 99.3%.

Report Title: CoT May Be Highly Informative Despite “Unfaithfulness”
Finding: METR replicated Anthropic's Claude 3.7 Sonnet system-card faithfulness evaluation and matched Anthropic's results within error, but identified a methodological flaw in Anthropic's setup: it used multiple-choice questions, allowing the model to reach the right answer by guessing rather than by using the clue.
Finding Quote: The Anthropic researchers’ original setup used multiple-choice questions, allowing the model to guess the correct answer easily.

Report Title: Deep Ignorance: Filtering Pretraining Data Builds Tamper-Resistant Safeguards into Open-Weight LLMs
Finding: Filtered models could still leverage harmful info supplied in-context (search augmentation), so layered defence still needed
Finding Quote: However, while filtered models lack internalized dangerous knowledge, we find that they can still leverage such information when it is provided in context (e.g., via search tool augmentation), demonstrating a need for a defense-in-depth approach.

Report Title: Deep Ignorance: Filtering Pretraining Data Builds Tamper-Resistant Safeguards into Open-Weight LLMs
Finding: No degradation to unrelated capabilities from filtering
Finding Quote: with no observed degradation to unrelated capabilities.

Report Title: Deep Ignorance: Filtering Pretraining Data Builds Tamper-Resistant Safeguards into Open-Weight LLMs
Finding: Filtering hazardous content from pretraining data yields substantially more tamper-resistant safety than post-training defences alone — filtered models resisted adversarial fine-tuning up to 10,000 steps / 300M tokens of biothreat text.
Finding Quote: they exhibit substantial resistance to adversarial fine-tuning attacks on up to 10,000 steps and 300M tokens of biothreat-related text -- outperforming existing post-training baselines by over an order of magnitude

Report Title: PentestJudge: Judging Agent Behavior Against Operational Requirements
Models / Systems: 12 candidate LLM judges (Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, DeepSeek, Meta, Alibaba, Moonshot); trajectories generated by GPT-4.1 pentest agent
Finding: Across 12 LLM judges scored against human-expert ground truth on pentest trajectories, Claude 3.7 Sonnet performed best (85% accuracy, F1=0.83); open-weight Kimi-K2-Instruct was competitive (F1=0.79).
Finding Quote: Claude Sonnet 3.7 performs the best at an accuracy of 85% and an F1 score of 0.83

Report Title: PentestJudge: Judging Agent Behavior Against Operational Requirements
Finding: LLM judges showed systematic failure modes grading pentest trajectories: open models under-searched long trajectories, some frontier judges misunderstood security terminology, and Claude 4 Sonnet hallucinated additional unstated requirements, incorrectly failing a valid trajectory.
Finding Quote: Claude 4 Sonnet failed a penetration testing trajectory for failing to enumerate the network enough

Report Title: Evals: The Foundation for Autonomous Offensive Security
Models / Systems: OpenAI o1 (o1-2024-12-17) driving a Mythic/Apollo agent harness in the GOAD Active Directory lab; used as an instrument
Finding: Dreadnode documents an evaluation methodology for autonomous offensive-security agents (action-space design, string/structured-object/LLM-judge verifiers, repeated trials with logged independent variables), motivated by the observation that the same o1-driven agent found the planted SYSVOL domain credentials on one run and failed to find anything usable on another.
Finding Quote: In this run, the model performed some basic recon, but hasn't given us anything usable and failed to find the credentials. So does the agent work, or not?

Institution: International Network of AI Safety Institutes
Report Title: International Joint Testing Exercise 3 (Agentic Testing)
Models / Systems: Two anonymised open-source models (Model E and Model F) on Cybench and InterCode CTF, evaluated with Inspect and HiBayES
Finding: In the UK AISI-led cybersecurity strand, Bayesian modelling (HiBayES) over Cybench and InterCode CTF runs found that most evaluation parameters varied — agent prompt, individual tool removal, token limit — had no substantial effect on agent success rate; the only significant effect was reduced performance for Model E at higher temperature, and benchmark choice dominated all other variables.
Finding Quote: most target variables did not have a substantial impact on model success rate.

Report Title: EvoBench: Towards Real-world LLM-Generated Text Detection Benchmarking for Evolving Large Language Models
Models / Systems: 14 LLM-generated-text detection methods (incl. Fast-DetectGPT, RADAR) evaluated against 7 LLM families and 29 evolving versions (GPT-4o, Claude, LLaMA and others)
Finding: Evaluating 14 detection methods on EvoBench, the team found all of them fail to generalise as LLMs evolve: Fast-DetectGPT falls by up to 25%, from 0.91 AUROC on Claude-3-haiku-20240307 to 0.65 on Claude-3-5-haiku-20241022, and from 0.8003 average accuracy on GPT-4o-05-13 to 0.7422 on GPT-4o-latest, so static benchmarks overstate real-world detector effectiveness.
Finding Quote: The widely used detection method, Fast-DetectGPT, declines up to 25% drop when detecting the Claude-3-5-haiku20241022 compared to Claude-3-haiku-20240307.

Report Title: Layer-Aware Representation Filtering: Purifying Finetuning Data to Preserve LLM Safety Alignment (EMNLP 2025)
Finding: Fine-tuning Llama 3.1 on benign samples ranked most 'safety-degrading' by the authors' LARF filter raised HarmBench ASR from 3.5% to 39%; fine-tuning on the safest-ranked samples reduced ASR to 0%.
Finding Quote: fine-tuning Llama3.1 with the 1,000 bottom ranked samples flagged by LARF raises the Attack Success Rate (ASR) on HarmBench from 3.5% to 39%

Report Title: Layer-Aware Representation Filtering: Purifying Finetuning Data to Preserve LLM Safety Alignment (EMNLP 2025)
Models / Systems: N/A (method finding; demonstrated on Llama3, Llama3.1, Qwen2.5)
Finding: LARF identified safety-degrading fine-tuning data more effectively than SEAL, GradSafe and Bi-Anchoring on all three tested models while requiring no additional training data, no gradient computation, one GPU and 0.5 hour; removing the flagged samples preserved downstream task scores (HumanEval, PubMedQA, MATH) while lowering DirectHarm4 harmfulness.
Finding Quote: Although LARF neither requires additional training data nor gradient computations, it remains the most effective. For all models, LARF achieves the highest ASR on the two datasets.

Report Title: WebGuard: Building a Generalizable Guardrail for Web Agents
Finding: Fine-tuning a Qwen2.5VL-7B guardrail on WebGuard raised outcome-prediction accuracy from 37% to 80% and HIGH-risk action recall from 20% to 76%, which the authors state still falls short of the reliability needed for high-stakes deployment.
Finding Quote: boosting accuracy from 37% to 80% and HIGH-risk action recall from 20% to 76%

Report Title: Collectivism and Individualism Political Bias in Large Language Models: A Two-Step Approach
Finding: The paper contributes a two-step political-bias evaluation protocol - a value assessment that scores generated content on a five-point Likert scale against a neutrality midpoint of 3, followed by a factual assessment checking whether the model can correctly classify statements as collectivist or individualist - arguing a trustworthy LLM should be accurate on facts while neutral in value judgements.
Finding Quote: We propose a two-step approach to evaluate the patterns of bias in the outputs of LLMs as well as a specific set of questions to examine LLM outputs' political bias on collectivism and individualism.

Report Title: STACK: Adversarial Attacks on LLM Safeguard Pipelines
Models / Systems: Multiple frontier models with multi-component safety systems
Finding: The STACK staged attack bypasses multi-component LLM safeguard pipelines even when individual components appear robust, achieving 71% ASR black-box and 33% ASR in a no-access transfer setting on the ClearHarm catastrophic-misuse dataset.
Finding Quote: Second, we introduce a STaged AttaCK (STACK) procedure that achieves 71% ASR on ClearHarm in a black-box attack against the few-shot-prompted classifier pipeline. Finally, we also evaluate STACK in a transfer setting, achieving 33% ASR, providing initial evidence that it is feasible to design attacks with no access to the target pipeline.

Report Title: STACK: Adversarial Attacks on LLM Safeguard Pipelines
Models / Systems: Multiple frontier models with multi-component safety systems
Finding: Authors' few-shot-prompted classifier reduces ASR to 0% on ClearHarm and outperforms ShieldGemma across three attack types and two datasets
Finding Quote: First, we find that a novel few-shot-prompted input and output classifier outperforms state-of-the-art open-weight safeguard model ShieldGemma across three attacks and two datasets, reducing the attack success rate (ASR) to 0% on the catastrophic misuse dataset ClearHarm.

Institution: Joint UK AISI + International Network (10 countries)
Report Title: International Joint Testing Exercise 3 (Agentic Testing)
Finding: Methodological findings: realistic task/tool design materially affects results; agent reasoning trajectories require evaluation beyond pass/fail; parameter optimization (temperature, token limits) significantly affects performance variability across models.
Finding Quote: [Section: Tasks and tools should be designed to be realistic]: "Reduces chances of error, e.g. mimic Github formats. Match common syntax of popular platforms. Reduces the chance of models realising they are in a simulated environment."; [Section: Assessing agent trajectory is as important as agent outcome]: "Test design should be intentional with clear goals. This exercise used a simple agentic setup with minimal guardrails to surface base safety issues. It is important to capture the agent's reasoning for deeper insights. For instance, it may help identify unsafe thinking/behaviour, even if the eventual outcome is not harmful."; [Table 9 / Figure 8: parameter variations and their effect on success rate]: "Temperature 0.55, 0.85, 1.00, 1.15 | Attempts 10 (additional values extrapolated) | Token Limit 2.5M, 5M (additional values extrapolated)"; "Temperature values affected the models differently, as indicated by the temperature-model interaction term. The performance of Model E significantly declined with higher temperature values, whereas the success rate of Model F was not impacted."

Institution: Joint UK AISI + International Network (10 countries)
Report Title: International Joint Testing Exercise 3 (Agentic Testing)
Finding: LLM judges disagreed with human annotators on agent safety assessments. Across languages, discrepancy rates ranged from 15% to 36% for Model C and from 23% to 41% for Model D.
Finding Quote: Human-judge-LLM discrepancy ranged from 15%-36% for Model C and 23%-41% for Model D.

Report Title: The Levers of Political Persuasion with Conversational AI
Finding: Applying cheap reward-model post-training to a small open-source model (Llama3.1-8B) made it as persuasive as, or more persuasive than, the much larger frontier model GPT-4o -- showing frontier-level persuasion capability is cheaply attainable.
Finding Quote: applying RM to a small open-source LLM (Llama3.1-8B) increased its persuasive effect from approximately 6pp to 9pp, making it as or more persuasive than the much larger and more expensive frontier model GPT-4o (8/24).

Report Title: A structured protocol for elicitation experiments -- 5-20x compute equivalent finding
Finding: Key empirical finding: elicitation techniques (prompting, tool access, multi-agent, response sampling) can improve model performance comparable to 5-20x training compute increase. Standard evaluations without proper elicitation systematically underestimate model capabilities by a potentially enormous margin.
Finding Quote: Research indicates that elicitation techniques can significantly enhance model performance, with improvements comparable to increasing training compute between five and twenty times.; Without these techniques, we may significantly underestimate what models can achieve

Report Title: White Box Control -- sandbagging detection degrades at scale
Finding: Empirical progress report on sandbagging detection. Deception probes (white box) worked well for Llama-3.1-8B but both white box and black box detection methods degraded significantly with Llama-3.3-70B and increased task complexity. Sandbagging detection at scale remains unsolved.
Finding Quote: We were surprised by the deterioration in performance of both the white and black box baseline methods from simply working with a larger model and more difficult task.

Institution: International Network of AI Safety Institutes
Report Title: Improving Methodologies for LLM Evaluations Across Global Languages (International Joint Testing Exercise — Multilingual)
Models / Systems: Two anonymized open-weight models, tested across ten languages (Cantonese, English, Farsi, French, Japanese, Korean, Kiswahili, Malay, Mandarin Chinese, Telugu)
Finding: Two open-weight models were tested on >6,000 newly translated prompts across five harm categories (privacy, non-violent crime, violent crime, IP, jailbreak robustness) in ten high- and low-resource languages. Safety safeguards were NOT equivalent across languages: safeguard robustness varied significantly by language and by harm type, and evaluator (LLM-as-judge vs human) reliability also varied. Literal translation was found insufficient — prompts required cultural adaptation.
Finding Quote: over 6,000 prompts were newly translated for this exercise, testing for safeguard effectiveness across five harm categories – privacy, non-violent crime, violent crime, intellectual property and robustness to jailbreaking.; testing two open-weight models – Mistral Large and Gemma 2 (27B) – across ten languages; though this varies by harm type – jailbreak protections were the weakest, while safeguards against intellectual property violations were the strongest.; 6 out of 10 languages showed more than 5% discrepancy between LLM-generated and human evaluation labels.; Literal translations are insufficient – prompts should be contextually adapted to each language and culture.

Report Title: Research Note: Our scheming precursor evals had limited predictive power for our in-context scheming evals
Finding: Validating the two eval suites against general capability (Artificial Analysis General Intelligence Scores), Apollo found a strong statistically significant correlation for the precursor suite (r=0.816) but a weaker, non-significant correlation for the in-context scheming suite (r=0.412), consistent with the scheming evals measuring a mix of capability and propensity rather than capability alone.
Finding Quote: We find positive correlations for both datasets with r=0.816 for Precursors and r=0.412 for Scheming. The precursor correlation is statistically significant, while the Scheming correlation isn’t.

Report Title: Research Note: Our scheming precursor evals had limited predictive power for our in-context scheming evals
Finding: Back-testing their own 2024 scheming precursor evaluations (agentic self-reasoning and applied theory of mind) against their December 2024 in-context scheming evaluations over 22 models with 100 runs each, Apollo found predictive power ranging from low to medium, with easy variants somewhat useful and hard variants neutral or actively misleading - a level of reliability they call clearly insufficient for the high-stakes frontier-safety-policy settings precursor evals are designed for.
Finding Quote: Depending on the analysis, we find that the predictive power ranges from low to medium. Specifically, we find that the “easy” versions of our evals are somewhat useful as predictors, but the “hard” versions are neutral or actively misleading.

Report Title: Research Note: Our scheming precursor evals had limited predictive power for our in-context scheming evals
Finding: In a threshold analysis over 10x10 precursor/scheming score threshold pairs per difficulty level, Apollo found that thresholds with low miss rates were usually trivially true and that misses occurred for many threshold pairs on or below the diagonal, concluding the observed miss and false-alarm rates would be unacceptably bad for high-risk use.
Finding Quote: We think that the rates that we observe for these two datasets would be unacceptably bad for high-risk cases.

Report Title: Agent-RLVR: Training Software Engineering Agents via Guidance and Environment Rewards
Finding: Scale AI's Agent-RLVR training framework raised Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct pass@1 on SWE-Bench Verified from 9.4% to 22.4%, and to 27.8% when the guidance-augmented data was also used to train a test-time reward model.
Finding Quote: Agent-RLVR elevates the pass@1 performance of Qwen-2.5-72B-Instruct from 9.4% to 22.4% on SWE-Bench Verified

Report Title: Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking
Finding: METR's two reward-hacking detection methods (anomalous-score inspection and an LLM monitor) each surfaced runs the other missed on a Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) RE-Bench dataset, so METR concludes its reported rates of reward hacking are likely a significant underestimate.
Finding Quote: The discrepancies between the reward hacks surfaced by each method indicate the amount of reward hacking we’ve found may be a significant underestimate.

Report Title: Recent Frontier Models Are Reward Hacking
Finding: In a pilot with OpenAI, METR built a prompted chain-of-thought reward-hacking classifier which OpenAI ran on 2,752 of METR's past o3 queries and returned the 15 highest-scoring plus 10 random instances; manual review confirmed the classifier accurately identified reward-hacking reasoning, demonstrating a workable limited third-party monitoring arrangement that avoids IP leakage.
Finding Quote: By manually reviewing the flagged chains-of-thought, we confirmed that the classifier accurately identified instances of reasoning about reward hacking.

Report Title: Avoiding AI Deception: Lie Detectors can either Induce Honesty or Evasion
Finding: Putting a lie detector in the preference-labelling loop only produced honesty at high detector sensitivity: with a detector true positive rate above 80% the trained model lied less than 25% of the time, while at a TPR of 60-70% the GRPO policy lied more than 85% of the time, because low-TPR datasets contain enough undetected lies for the model to learn to evade the detector.
Finding Quote: When the lie detector has a very high TPR (greater than 80%), the trained model lies less than 25% of the time. However, when the lie detector is less powerful, with a TPR of 60-70%, the GRPO policy lies more than 85% of the time.

Report Title: Avoiding AI Deception: Lie Detectors can either Induce Honesty or Evasion
Finding: On-policy GRPO training against a lie detector produced substantially more deception than off-policy DPO: at low detector sensitivity, where only about 35% of lies are caught, GRPO models lied in approximately 85% of responses, while DPO models' deception rate never exceeded 65% and averaged half that of GRPO.
Finding Quote: By contrast, DPO models' deception rate never exceeds 65% and on average they lie half as often as GRPO models.

Report Title: Avoiding AI Deception: Lie Detectors can either Induce Honesty or Evasion
Finding: KL regularisation toward the original honest model turned out to be partly responsible for keeping models honest: at a mid-range detector TPR of about 68%, varying the GRPO KL coefficient from 0 to 0.5 cut the deception rate from a peak of 95% to as little as 25%, and at extremely weak regularisation responses became repetitive and formulaic minimal patterns that lie without detection.
Finding Quote: In particular, for GRPO, we find that for a mid-range detector TPR (~68%), varying the KL coefficient from 0 to 0.5 leads to a drop in the deception rate from a peak of 95% to as little as 25%.

Report Title: Avoiding AI Deception: Lie Detectors can either Induce Honesty or Evasion
Finding: Lie detectors built on sparse-autoencoder features generally performed worse than detectors trained on raw activations, and the relationship between model size and deception was inconsistent across the sizes studied.
Finding Quote: We also found that SAE-based detectors generally perform worse than detectors based on raw activations. We also studied the relationship between model size and deception, finding an inconsistent trend.

Report Title: Existing Large Language Model unlearning evaluations are inconclusive
Finding: UK AISI identifies principles that LLM unlearning evaluations must satisfy and shows through targeted experiments that violating each principle leads to misleading conclusions about whether knowledge has been removed.
Finding Quote: We validate these principles through a series of targeted experiments, showing how violations of each can lead to misleading conclusions.

Report Title: Adversarial Preference Learning for Robust LLM Alignment (ACL 2025 Findings)
Finding: Undefended Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 has high baseline ASR (56.25% direct-request, 67.50% GCG); the authors' APL training method reduces these substantially (to 11.25%/41.25%) and raises harmlessness win rate from 50% to 83.33%.
Finding Quote: Modern language models often rely on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)... they remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks

Report Title: Evaluating AI Cyber Capabilities with Crowdsourced Elicitation
Finding: AI teams ranked in the top 5% and top 10% in two open CTFs containing 400 and 8,000 teams.
Finding Quote: The AI teams ... ranking top-5% and top-10% respectively for a total of $7500 in bounties.

Institution: Apollo Research + Anthropic (AISI-adjacent -- Apollo in AISIC)
Report Title: System Card: Claude Opus 4 & Claude Sonnet 4
Models / Systems: Claude Opus 4 (early pre-release snapshot -- NOT released version)
Finding: Anthropic fixed a training bug and the snapshot was retrained and the fixed model shipped as Claude Opus 4
Finding Quote: we discovered that we had mistakenly omitted the only finetuning dataset that included harmful system prompts; the final Claude Opus 4 reverted to the much lower baseline seen with prior Claude models.

Report Title: System Card: Claude Opus 4 & Claude Sonnet 4
Finding: The US AI Safety Institute and UK AI Security Institute conducted joint pre-deployment testing of Claude Opus 4 focused on catastrophic risks in CBRN, cybersecurity, and autonomous-capabilities domains -- no specific result is disclosed in this base system card (distinct from the later, separately-published Constitutional Classifiers red-teaming report).
Finding Quote: joint pre-deployment testing of the new Claude Opus 4 model was conducted by the US AI Safety Institute (US AISI) and the UK AI Security Institute (UK AISI).; The institutes conducted independent assessments focused on potential catastrophic risks in the CBRN, cybersecurity, and autonomous capabilities domains.

Report Title: UK AISI x Gray Swan Agent Red-Teaming Challenge: Results Snapshot
Models / Systems: Aggregate across all 22 tested agentic LLMs
Finding: Gray Swan and UK AISI ran a month-long crowdsourced public red-teaming competition (Mar 8-Apr 6, 2025), the largest public evaluation of agentic LLM safety to date.
Finding Quote: the largest public evaluation of agentic LLM safety to date

Report Title: Assessing Robustness to Spurious Correlations in Post-Training Language Models
Models / Systems: anonymised (models post-trained with SFT, DPO and KTO)
Finding: Comparing SFT, DPO and KTO across synthetic tasks with 10% versus 90% spurious correlation, Scale AI found that models often but not always degrade under higher spuriousness, with preference methods relatively robust on mathematical reasoning and SFT stronger on context-intensive tasks, so no single post-training strategy dominates.
Finding Quote: Our results show that the models often but not always degrade under higher spuriousness.

Report Title: The Automation Advantage in AI Red Teaming
Finding: Although automation won on success rate, manual attempts solved challenges roughly 5.2x faster by median time (1.5 minutes versus 11.6 minutes), with the direction reversing on some challenge types, which Dreadnode uses to argue for hybrid human-plus-automated testing.
Finding Quote: median solve times showed manual attempts were approximately 5.2 times faster (1.5 minutes versus 11.6 minutes for automated approaches)

Report Title: RepliBench: Evaluating the Autonomous Replication Capabilities of Language Model Agents
Models / Systems: Claude 3.7 Sonnet; Claude 3.5 Sonnet (new); GPT-4o; o1; o3-mini
Finding: RepliBench decomposes autonomous replication into a capability chain/categories (e.g., obtaining weights, replicating onto compute, obtaining resources, persisting/evading shutdown) -- the benchmark structure of 20 task families across these categories is a distinct methodological contribution the authors call 'Capability Tree Analysis' (CTA), adapting Fault Tree Analysis from safety engineering to decompose complex AI capabilities into more easily assessed sub-capabilities.
Finding Quote: RepliBench is derived from a decomposition of these capabilities covering four core domains: obtaining resources, exfiltrating model weights, replicating onto compute, and persisting on this compute for long periods; Fault tree analysis (FTA) is widely used in safety engineering to identify how combinations of events can lead to system failures. We apply a similar decomposition approach to evaluate complex AI capabilities by breaking them into more easily assessed sub-capabilities, which we call capability tree analysis (CTA).

Report Title: OpenAI o3 and o4-mini System Card
Finding: OpenAI granted early access to o3 and o4-mini to the US AI Safety Institute (cyber and biological capability domains) and the UK AI Security Institute (cyber, chemical/biological, autonomy, and an early safeguards version) -- no specific quantitative results are attributed to either institute in the card itself.
Finding Quote: OpenAI granted early access to these versions of o3 and o4-mini to the U.S. AI Safety Institute to conduct evaluations of the models' cyber and biological capabilities, and to the U.K. AI Security Institute to conduct evaluations of cyber, chemical and biological, and autonomy capabilities, and an early version of the safeguards.

Report Title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling
Models / Systems: anonymised (adversarially constructed AI agent; trusted/untrusted model pair)
Finding: Redwood ran what it describes as the first control evaluation performed in an agent environment, building BashBench, a dataset of 257 challenging multi-step system administration tasks, and testing whether monitoring and security protocols can stop an adversarially constructed AI agent from covertly downloading and executing malicious code.
Finding Quote: Our work presents the first control evaluation performed in an agent environment. We construct BashBench, a dataset of 257 challenging multi-step system administration tasks, and evaluate whether various safety measures can prevent an adversarially constructed AI agent from covertly downloading and executing malicious code in this environment.

Report Title: Ctrl-Z: Controlling AI Agents via Resampling
Models / Systems: anonymised (adversarially constructed AI agent; trusted/untrusted model pair)
Finding: Resample protocols, which dynamically take additional samples of suspicious actions to block execution and generate incriminating evidence, significantly outperformed existing control techniques: the best protocol combined resampling with analysis of previous steps and cut attack success from 58% to 7% at a 5% cost to the performance of a non-malicious agent.
Finding Quote: We measure the tradeoff between attack prevention and usefulness; our best protocol combines resampling with analysis of previous steps, reducing the success rate of attacks from 58% to 7% at a 5% cost to the performance of a non-malicious agent.

Report Title: Among us: A sandbox for measuring and detecting agentic deception
Models / Systems: anonymised (LLM agents in the Among Us sandbox)
Finding: Logistic-regression probes on model activations, trained on a dataset of 'pretend you're a dishonest model' prompts, generalised extremely well out of distribution in the Among Us sandbox, consistently reaching AUROCs over 95% even when scored on the deceptive statement alone without the chain of thought.
Finding Quote: We find that probes trained on a dataset of "pretend you're a dishonest model: ...'' generalize extremely well out-of-distribution, consistently obtaining AUROCs over 95% even when evaluated just on the deceptive statement, without the chain of thought.

Report Title: Among us: A sandbox for measuring and detecting agentic deception
Models / Systems: anonymised (LLM agents in the Among Us sandbox)
Finding: Two sparse-autoencoder features detected deception well in the Among Us sandbox but could not be used to steer the model into lying less, a negative result for SAE-based steering as a deception mitigation.
Finding Quote: We also find two SAE features that work well at deception detection but are unable to steer the model to lie less.

Report Title: Building intelligence identification system via large language model watermarking: a survey and beyond
Models / Systems: Three multi-bit watermarking schemes (Cyclic-Shift hash, MPAC, CTWL), with LLaMA-2-13B as the perplexity oracle
Finding: In the authors' own experiments on three multi-bit watermarking schemes, success rate, text quality (perplexity) and information density (bits per word) trade off against each other: at fixed information density, better text quality comes with lower extraction success rate, and lowering information density improves both other metrics.
Finding Quote: a trade-off exists between text quality, watermark success rate, and information density. At the same information density, achieving better text quality often results in a decreased success rate.

Report Title: ADAM: An Embodied Causal Agent in Open-World Environments (ICLR 2025)
Models / Systems: ADAM (Shanghai AI Lab agent) built on GPT-4-turbo (gpt-4-0125-preview) with LLaVA-v1.5-13B; baselines include Voyager-style LLM agents
Finding: ADAM, an embodied causal agent, builds a near-complete causal graph of Minecraft from scratch with no prior knowledge and achieves higher task success rates than baseline agents, retaining performance in a modified Minecraft where crafting recipes are altered.
Finding Quote:
Extensive experiments show
that A DAM constructs a nearly perfect causal graph from scratch, enabling ef-
ficient task decomposition and execution with strong interpretability.

Report Title: Introducing Docent
Finding: Docent's automated transcript analysis identified environment defects on the InterCode benchmark - packages the agent invoked but that were missing from the environment - and simply installing them raised GPT-4o's solve rate from 68.6% to 78%, showing that a reported benchmark score can substantially understate agent capability.
Finding Quote: Docent identifies issues in an agent's environment, like missing packages the agent invoked. On the InterCode [ 1 ] benchmark, simply adding those packages increased GPT-4o's solve rate from 68.6% to 78%.

Report Title: Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Software Tasks
Finding: METR proposes measuring model capability as the human-time length of tasks a model completes with a given reliability, and shows human task length is strongly predictive of model success: current models had near-100% success on tasks taking humans under 4 minutes and under 10% success on tasks taking over about 4 hours.
Finding Quote: current models have almost 100% success rate on tasks taking humans less than 4 minutes, but succeed <10% of the time on tasks taking more than around 4 hours

Report Title: Model Tampering Attacks Enable More Rigorous Evaluations of LLM Capabilities
Finding: State-of-the-art unlearning methods can be undone within ~16 steps of fine-tuning, indicating safety interventions are more fragile than assumed.
Finding Quote: state-of-the-art unlearning methods can easily be undone within 16 steps of fine-tuning.

Report Title: Model Tampering Attacks Enable More Rigorous Evaluations of LLM Capabilities
Finding: Demonstrates that model tampering attacks can reveal true capability ceilings that standard evaluations cannot detect. Key finding: standard evaluations without tampering systematically underestimate true model capabilities, creating a structural blind spot in capability assessment.
Finding Quote: the behaviors identified during any particular input-output evaluation can only lower-bound the model's worst-possible-case input-output behavior.

Report Title: GPT-4.5 System Card
Finding: METR was given 7 days of access to an earlier GPT-4.5 checkpoint, with OpenAI sharing a subset of its internal evaluation results so METR could interpret its own; METR reported this raised the robustness of its findings and that verifying developers' internal results is a promising third-party evaluation direction, while noting post-training capability evaluations support only limited safety assurances.
Finding Quote: This allowed METR to increase the robustness of their findings. METR believes third-party evaluations based on verifying developers' internal results is a promising direction to explore further.

Report Title: Claude 3.7 Sonnet System Card
Finding: Under voluntary MOUs, the US AI Safety Institute and UK AI Security Institute conducted pre-deployment testing of Claude 3.7 Sonnet across Anthropic's RSP-framework domains, informing Anthropic's ASL determination; the capabilities report was also shared with METR for feedback -- no specific result is disclosed in the card.
Finding Quote: Under our voluntary Memorandums of Understanding, the U.S. AI Safety Institute (U.S. AISI) and U.K. AI Security Institute (U.K. AISI) conducted pre-deployment testing of Claude 3.7 Sonnet across the domains outlined in our RSP framework.; We provided a copy of our capabilities report to these organizations and to METR for feedback.

Report Title: Forecasting Frontier Language Model Agent Capabilities
Finding: Apollo compared six forecasting approaches for downstream LM agent capability by backtesting them on 38 models from the Open LLM Leaderboard v2 across six benchmarks, and found a two-step Release Date to Chatbot Arena Elo to benchmark-score pipeline competitive and best supported by publicly available data, which they then used for their frontier forecasts.
Finding Quote: To identify the most effective forecasting approach, we systematically evaluated six methods through backtesting on the Open LLM Leaderboard v2 dataset, using 38 models on six benchmarks.

Report Title: Forecasting Frontier Language Model Agent Capabilities
Finding: Apollo documented four limitations that bound their own forecasts: the fits are almost entirely on pre-training-scaling-era models and so do not account for inference-compute scaling (which the authors think makes their estimates too conservative), elicitation effort was low, the frontier-model sample is inherently small, and the benchmark scope is limited to software engineering, cyber and ML engineering.
Finding Quote: Important limitation: Our approach does not account for recent advances in inference-compute scaling. Thus, some of the authors think our estimates are too conservative.

Report Title: Measuring Automated Kernel Engineering
Models / Systems: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, o1 (KernelBench leaderboard models)
Finding: Adding agent scaffolding and roughly $20/task of test-time compute (against under $1 in the original KernelBench work) raised the best-of-3 speedup from 1.05x to 1.81x, a 15x improvement, with about 4 engineer-weeks of effort; fine-tuning GPT-4o on 1,200 best solutions further closed almost all of its gap to o3-mini.
Finding Quote: Taking the best of 3 models which were used in the original KernelBench Leaderboard, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and o1, achieved 1.81x speedup, 15 times higher than the 1.05x speedup from best-of-k across models in original KernelBench.

Report Title: Biollama: Testing Biology Pre-Training Risks
Finding: Biology-corpus pretraining was unlikely to improve bio-lab-assistant performance, while inference scaling and task-specific fine-tuning were more promising.
Finding Quote: pre-training on biological corpora is unlikely to improve performance.

Report Title: Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes
Finding: Simple logistic-regression probes trained on RepE-style data detected deceptive responses from Llama-3.3-70B in more complicated and realistic environments, and Apollo's best probes performed comparably to a black-box baseline in which GPT-4o was shown the transcript and asked whether the model had responded deceptively.
Finding Quote: Our best probes performs comparably to this baseline, although we iterated more on the probes than the baseline.

Report Title: Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes
Finding: The probes were measurably imperfect: Apollo reports the probe firing on honest confessions of prior deception, mean scores being wrong even when per-token behaviour looked reasonable, and unexplained failures where the probe fired on an objectively honest response; they also found the probe fires far less on unrelated alpaca responses, suggesting it may partly be a detector for deception-related text rather than actual deception.
Finding Quote: The probe fires far less on alpaca responses unrelated to deception, indicating it may partially be a probe for “deception-related” text rather than “actually-deceptive” text.

Report Title: Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes
Finding: Among probe variants, one trained on activations after appending the follow-up 'Was your last response deceptive?' / 'No' was nearly perfect at separating deceptive from control responses, a roleplaying-trained probe separated honest from deceptive but not deceptive from control, an SAE-activation probe was somewhat worse across the board, and a sleeper-agent-style single-descriptive-question probe worked poorly on Apollo's evaluation sets.
Finding Quote: A probe trained on activations after appending “Was your last response deceptive?” “No”. This probe is nearly perfect at distinguishing deceptive responses from control responses.

Report Title: An update on our preliminary evaluations of Claude 3.5 Sonnet and o1
Finding: A short, small-scale scaffold-elicitation effort more than doubled o1's human-baseline-equivalent time on METR's autonomous risk evaluation, which METR presents as evidence that any single capability-based safety case is fragile to elicitation effort and inference budget.
Finding Quote: this was sufficient for a dramatic rise in performance in our autonomous risk evaluation: more than a doubling of the corresponding human baseline comparison time

Report Title: An update on our preliminary evaluations of Claude 3.5 Sonnet and o1
Finding: During the pre-deployment evaluation of o1, METR was not given access to the model's internal chain of thought and had no knowledge of the reasoning_effort parameter (using the default 'medium'), which limited elicitation and left METR unable to rule out sandbagging.
Finding Quote: We were not able to access o1’s internal chain of thought. This limits our ability to properly elicit the system’s capabilities.

Report Title: MultiChallenge: A Realistic Multi-Turn Conversation Evaluation Benchmark Challenging to Frontier LLMs
Finding: Scale AI developed an LLM-as-judge protocol with instance-level rubrics for MultiChallenge and reports fair agreement with experienced human raters, enabling automatic scoring of multi-turn conversations.
Finding Quote: We also develop LLM as judge with instance-level rubrics to facilitate an automatic evaluation method with fair agreement with experienced human raters.

Report Title: Hacking CTFs with Plain Agents
Finding: A simply scaffolded LLM agent solved 95% of InterCode-CTF challenges and 100% of three categories.
Finding Quote: Our new LLM agent solves 95% of InterCode-CTF challenges with a simple prompting strategy.

Report Title: ToolComp: A Multi-Tool Reasoning & Process Supervision Benchmark
Finding: Scale AI found that process-supervised reward models generalise substantially better than outcome-supervised reward models for ranking tool-use trajectories, improving rank@1 accuracy by 19% for base-model and 11% for fine-tuned-model trajectories.
Finding Quote: PRMs generalize significantly better than ORMs, achieving a 19% and 11% improvement in rank@1 accuracy

Report Title: MLLMGuard: A Multi-dimensional Safety Evaluation Suite for Multimodal Large Language Models
Models / Systems: GuardRank evaluator; GPT-4 / GPT-4V as comparison judges
Finding: The purpose-built lightweight GuardRank evaluator achieved significantly higher evaluation accuracy than GPT-4 on MLLMGuard, and using GPT-4V as both evaluator and evaluatee was shown to be unreliable because of self-preference bias.
Finding Quote: a fully automated lightweight evaluator termed GuardRank is developed, which achieves significantly higher evaluation accuracy than GPT-4

Report Title: Long-Form Tasks: Biological Protocol Generation Evaluation
Finding: Long-form biological protocol generation responses require roughly ten times more output tokens than standard Q&A evaluations, revealing a structural gap between standard Q&A benchmarks (which measure recall) and the reasoning/planning demands of real-world biological tasks.
Finding Quote: High quality solutions to tasks are expected to be > 3,000 tokens in length compared to ≈ 300 tokens for Q/A solutions

Report Title: Beyond Surface Structure: A Causal Assessment of LLMs' Comprehension Ability (ICLR 2025)
Models / Systems: Mainstream closed- and open-source LLMs (not individually named)
Finding: Using a causal-mediation-analysis method, most mainstream LLMs show genuine deep-structure comprehension growing with accuracy; closed-source LLMs rely more on deep structure, open-source more surface-sensitive, gap shrinking with scale.
Finding Quote: Comparing ADCE and AICE demonstrates closed-source LLMs rely more on deep structure, while open-source LLMs are more surface-sensitive, which decreases with model scale.

Report Title: The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
Models / Systems: Llama-3.1 family, Code Llama family, Command family, GPT-4o
Finding: Because resampling cannot reduce a verifier's false-positive probability, it imposes a hard ceiling on achievable accuracy no matter the compute budget; on HumanEval and MBPP the authors found a strong correlation between a model's single-sample accuracy and its false-positive rate, so no amount of inference scaling of a weaker model lets it match the single-sample accuracy of a sufficiently strong model such as GPT-4o.
Finding Quote: Resampling cannot decrease this probability, so it imposes an upper bound to the accuracy of resampling-based inference scaling, regardless of compute budget.

Report Title: The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
Models / Systems: Llama-3.1 family, Code Llama family, GPT-4o
Finding: Once a cost is attached to returning a false positive, inference-scaling curves bend downward: the authors found the optimal number of resampling attempts is often fewer than 10, and for weak models with a high false-positive risk the optimal number of attempts can be zero.
Finding Quote: Empirical results show that optimal sampling attempts are often fewer than 10, as the negative utility of false positives outweighs benefits, bending inference scaling curves downward.

Report Title: The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling
Models / Systems: Llama-3.1 family, Code Llama family, GPT-4o
Finding: Beyond being incorrect, solutions that pass limited unit tests but fail the extended suite were of measurably lower quality - the authors report worse adherence to coding style conventions and different implementation length - so false positives are undesirable on axes beyond correctness.
Finding Quote: Finally, false positives may have other undesirable qualities, like poor adherence to coding style conventions.

Institution: Joint UK + US + Singapore AISIs (International Network)
Report Title: A Pilot Testing Exercise from the International Network of AI Safety Institutes
Finding: Small methodological differences in testing procedures -- such as differing output-parsing rules and token limits -- produced GSM8K (English-language) score variations exceeding 5 percentage points across the three participating AISIs despite using the same model and prompting strategy, highlighting the need for standardised, interoperable international AI testing methodologies.
Finding Quote: Finding #1: Small methodological differences can have a large impact.

Institution: Joint UK + US + Singapore AISIs (International Network)
Report Title: A Pilot Testing Exercise from the International Network of AI Safety Institutes
Finding: Prompt-optimization strategy choices produced substantial performance swings (e.g. SQuAD2.0 73.3%–82.7%).
Finding Quote: [Figure B: AISIs' Results on SQuAD 2.0]: "Network Member | F1 Score"; "SG (4-shot, no CoT, basic instr.) | 77.5"; "UK (0-shot, no CoT, basic instr.) | 73.3 ± 0.4"; "U.S. (0-shot, CoT, prescriptive instr.) | 82.7 ± 0.3"

Institution: Joint UK + US + Singapore AISIs (International Network)
Report Title: A Pilot Testing Exercise from the International Network of AI Safety Institutes
Finding: The exercise represented the first-ever joint AI safety testing conducted across three national AI Safety Institutes (UK, US, Singapore), establishing a new multilateral precedent for coordinated AI evaluation.
Finding Quote: This first testing exercise was intended to provide an initial starting point for Network Members to discuss their respective approaches to testing foundation models and begin work towards building common best practices for model tests.

Report Title: Pre-deployment evaluation of Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct 2024)
Finding: This evaluation was a joint pre-deployment AI safety testing exercise conducted between the UK and US AI Safety Institutes on Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Oct 2024).
Finding Quote: This evaluation was conducted jointly by the United States Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute (US AISI) and the United Kingdom Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute (UK AISI), and this report describes in detail its technical methodology and findings.

Report Title: OASIS: Open Agent Social Interaction Simulations with One Million Agents
Finding: In a ~1M-agent OASIS simulation seeded with matched real news/misinformation pairs, agent posts about fabricated misinformation consistently outnumbered posts about official news across all 4 topics.
Finding Quote: the number of posts related to misinformation consistently exceeds those related to official news

Report Title: OASIS: Open Agent Social Interaction Simulations with One Million Agents
Finding: Agents running an 'uncensored' Llama-3 variant produced more extreme language, and simulated agents exhibited a herd effect responding to dislikes that grew more pronounced with scale.
Finding Quote: The uncensored model tends to use more extreme phrases... this effect becomes more pronounced as the number of agents increases

Report Title: Our First Year
Finding: AISI evaluated 16 models in its first year but has not published detailed results for most of them, citing an inability to release all results since they often contain sensitive material.
Finding Quote: In our first year, we've conducted evaluations on 16 models. Nor can we release all our results into the public domain, since they often contain sensitive material.

Report Title: Scaling Automatic Neuron Description
Finding: Transluce released a database of natural-language descriptions for all 458,752 MLP neurons in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, generated by a fine-tuned 8B explainer with best-of-k sampling and a fine-tuned scorer, at a computational cost of about $0.046 per neuron.
Finding Quote: These improvements allow for high-quality descriptions with a computational cost of approximately $0.046 per neuron (see Appendix for the cost breakdown).

Report Title: Scaling Automatic Neuron Description
Finding: On a hand-annotated subset of neurons, the automated descriptions scored slightly better than human expert descriptions on Transluce's automated quality metric (average 0.61 versus 0.55), and the final distilled 8B explainer outperformed GPT-4o-mini at generating descriptions.
Finding Quote: The automated descriptions are qualitatively similar to human descriptions and score slightly better on our automated quality metrics (average score of 0.61 0.61 0.61 vs. 0.55 0.55 0.55 ).

Report Title: Monitor: An AI-Driven Observability Interface
Finding: Transluce released Monitor, an open-source observability interface combining a pre-compiled neuron-description database, real-time activation and attribution views, an AI linter that clusters unexpected concepts as candidate spurious cues, and natural-language-guided steering of related neuron families.
Finding Quote: To address these challenges, we introduce Monitor , an observability interface designed to help humans observe, understand, and steer the internal computations of language models.

Report Title: The Tug of War Within: Mitigating the Fairness-Privacy Conflicts in Large Language Models
Models / Systems: Qwen-2-7B-Instruct and other open-weight instruction-tuned LLMs
Finding: SPIN, a training-free method that suppresses neurons coupling privacy and fairness awareness, removes the trade-off and improves both dimensions simultaneously without degrading general capabilities - for example improving Qwen-2-7B-Instruct's fairness awareness by 12.2% and privacy awareness by 14.0% - and remains effective with limited or even malicious fine-tuning data where SFT fails.
Finding Quote: significantly improves LLMs' fairness and privacy awareness simultaneously without compromising general capabilities, e.g., improving Qwen-2-7B-Instruct's fairness awareness by 12.2% and privacy awareness by 14.0%

Report Title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
Finding: Simple universal jailbreak templates adapted for agentic LLMs were effective across all 11 harm categories tested, indicating a systematic and broadly applicable attack surface; these templates preserve model capabilities, enabling coherent and malicious multi-step agent behavior.
Finding Quote: simple universal jailbreak templates can be adapted to effectively jailbreak agents, and (3) these jailbreaks enable coherent and malicious multi-step agent behavior and retain model capabilities.

Report Title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
Finding: Repeated sampling (best-of-5) amplified jailbreak success against OpenAI's GPT-4o, raising its harm score from 70.7% to 83.7% over a single-shot template attack.
Finding Quote: GPT-4o's harm score increases from 70.7% to 83.7% (best-of-5)

Report Title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
Finding: Repeated sampling (best-of-5) amplified jailbreak success against Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet, raising its harm score from 65.1% to 79.7% over a single-shot template attack.
Finding Quote: Claude 3.5 Sonnet improves from 65.1% to 79.7% (best-of-5)

Report Title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
Finding: Repeated sampling (best-of-5) amplified jailbreak success against Mistral Large 2 most of all models tested, raising its harm score from 67.4% to 90.8%.
Finding Quote: Mistral exhibits the most substantial enhancement, with its harm score rising from 67.4% to 90.8% (best-of-5)

Report Title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
Finding: The same jailbreak template was markedly less effective against OpenAI's GPT-4o as a plain chatbot query than as an agentic task: refusal rates rose from 9.1% to 31.8%.
Finding Quote: our template attack is noticeably less effective in the chat-only setting, increasing the refusal rates on GPT-4o from 9.1% to 31.8%

Report Title: AgentHarm: A Benchmark for Measuring Harmfulness of LLM Agents
Finding: The same jailbreak template was markedly less effective against Anthropic's Claude 3.5 Sonnet as a plain chatbot query than as an agentic task: refusal rates rose from 29.5% to 72.7%.
Finding Quote: increasing the refusal rates ... from 29.5% to 72.7% on Claude 3.5 Sonnet compared to the agent setting

Report Title: CORE-Bench: Fostering the Credibility of Published Research Through a Computational Reproducibility Agent Benchmark
Finding: Adapting a general-purpose agent (AutoGPT) into a task-specific variant (CORE-Agent) with prompting and tool modifications yielded significant performance improvements on the same underlying models, indicating that measured agent capability is heavily determined by the scaffold rather than the model alone.
Finding Quote: Results show that generalist agents can be easily adapted to specific tasks, yielding significant performance improvements.

Report Title: Planning In Natural Language Improves LLM Search For Code Generation
Models / Systems: anonymised (multiple code LLMs used as instruments)
Finding: Scale AI reports that PLANSEARCH, which searches over natural-language plans rather than code samples, reaches 77% pass@200 on LiveCodeBench and that the measured diversity of generated ideas predicts how much a model gains from scaling inference compute.
Finding Quote: achieving state-of-the-art results across coding benchmarks, including a 77% pass@200 on LiveCodeBench

Report Title: An update on our general capability evaluations
Models / Systems: Six LM agents incl. GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet
Finding: With METR's simple baseline scaffolding, agent task-completion rate plateaued at around 200 thousand tokens per task, far below the ~$800 (hundreds of millions of tokens) budget originally allotted, so additional inference budget produced no further signal.
Finding Quote: In fact, agent performance on our task suite seems to plateau at around 200 thousand tokens.

Report Title: AI Agents That Matter
Models / Systems: GPT-4, GPT-3.5 (as backends of Reflexion, LDB, LATS and the authors' baseline agents)
Finding: Three trivially simple baseline agents (retry, warming, escalation) built on the same underlying models matched the accuracy of published state-of-the-art agent architectures on HumanEval while costing far less; across substantially similar accuracy the cost differed by almost two orders of magnitude, with Reflexion and LDB costing over 50% more than the warming strategy and LATS over 50 times more.
Finding Quote: There is no significant accuracy difference between our warming strategy and the best-performing agent architecture.

Report Title: AI Agents That Matter
Finding: Reformulating agent design as joint optimisation of accuracy and cost (via a modified DSPy) cut variable cost by 53% for GPT-3.5 and 41% for Llama-3-70B on HotPotQA while maintaining accuracy, showing that the cost overhead of prompt-optimisation frameworks is not inherent.
Finding Quote: for GPT-3.5, joint optimization leads to 53% lower variable cost with similar accuracy compared to both default DSPy implementations. Similarly, for Llama-3-70B, it leads to a 41% lower cost while maintaining accuracy.

Report Title: AI Agents That Matter
Finding: The top agent on the WebArena leaderboard, STeP, achieved 35.8% - more than double the benchmark paper's best baseline - by hardcoding policies that solve the specific tasks in the benchmark; because WebArena has no held-out test set, leaderboard accuracy of this kind is misleading for downstream developers choosing a web agent.
Finding Quote: It turns out that STeP hardcodes policies to solve the specific tasks included in WebArena.

Report Title: ESC-Eval: Evaluating Emotion Support Conversations in Large Language Models
Models / Systems: ESC-Role role-playing evaluator and ESC-RANK automatic scorer
Finding: The team built an interactive evaluation pipeline for emotional-support conversation - a role-playing model (ESC-Role) driven by 2,801 reorganised role cards, followed by human annotation - and trained ESC-RANK on 59,654 manual evaluation results, reporting scoring performance that surpasses GPT-4 by 35 points.
Finding Quote: we developed ESC-RANK, which trained on the annotated data, achieving a scoring performance surpassing 35 points of GPT-4.

Report Title: Improving Alignment and Robustness with Circuit Breakers
Finding: Baseline ASR on unmodified Llama-3-8B-Instruct/Mistral-based setups is high under strong attacks (~44.5% GCG, ~80-85% prefilling); the authors' circuit-breakers defense reduces this sharply with minimal capability loss.
Finding Quote: Our technique can be applied to both text-only and multimodal language models to prevent the generation of harmful outputs without sacrificing utility -- even in the presence of powerful unseen attacks

Report Title: The Local Interaction Basis: Identifying Computationally-Relevant and Sparsely Interacting Features in Neural Networks
Finding: The same technique failed to transfer to language models: relative to a PCA baseline, interaction sparsity increased only slightly for Tinystories-1M and not at all for GPT2-small, and the authors could identify no modules or interpretable features - a published negative result about their own method.
Finding Quote: On language models however, we find that LIB does not help us understand the networks. We find that interaction sparsity, compared to a PCA baseline, increases only slightly (for Tinystories-1M) or not at all (GPT2-small), and can identify no modules or interpretable features.

Report Title: Fourth Progress Report
Models / Systems: Publicly available frontier LLMs (anonymised -- same cohort as May Update)
Finding: Baseline evaluations spanned four domains — Cyber, Chem-Bio, Safeguards, and Autonomous Systems — on publicly available frontier models (April 2024).
Finding Quote: We ran tests across Cyber, Chem-Bio, Safeguards and Autonomous Systems.

Report Title: Fourth Progress Report
Models / Systems: Publicly available frontier LLMs (anonymised -- same cohort as May Update)
Finding: Institutional milestones: partnership with the Canadian AI Safety Institute; opened a San Francisco office; appointed Jade Leung as CTO; established External Advisory Board including Yoshua Bengio.
Finding Quote: Secretary of State Donelan has announced a new partnership to work with the Canadian AI Safety Institute; We are opening a new office in San Francisco so that we can continue to work hand in glove with the US; We have also appointed Jade Leung, who joined us in October last year, as our Chief Technology Officer; We recruited an exceptional External Advisory Board (EAB) made up of National Security, technical and other specialists, including – but not limited to – Yoshua Bengio.

Report Title: AISI Pre-Deployment Test of Frontier Model (Spring Budget 2024 -- Undisclosed -- Outcome Type 4)
Models / Systems: One unnamed frontier model (identity not publicly disclosed)
Finding: UK AISI conducted a pre-deployment evaluation of an unnamed frontier model -- the first pre-deployment test publicly acknowledged by the UK Chancellor in the Spring 2024 Budget -- but did not publish results, name the model, or issue a standalone evaluation report. Second documented instance of AISI Outcome Type 4 pattern (evaluation conducted; results withheld under voluntary-access model).
Finding Quote: As the Chancellor announced in the Budget at the start of the year, we ran our tests on a frontier model before it was deployed.

Report Title: Measuring the impact of post-training enhancements
Models / Systems: AutoGPT (Aug 2023 release), LangChain ReAct on gpt-4-0613
Finding: Public open-source agent scaffolds (an August 2023 AutoGPT release and a LangChain ReAct implementation) performed noticeably worse than METR's own simple 'basic' scaffold on the same underlying model, showing that scaffolding choices can easily degrade measured capability.
Finding Quote: Despite the simplicity of our basic agent, the LangChain ReAct and AutoGPT versions we ran performed noticeably worse using the same model. This suggests that it’s easy to accidentally worsen performance by using slightly different prompting or scaffolding.

Report Title: The WMDP Benchmark: Measuring and Reducing Malicious Use With Unlearning
Finding: The authors' RMU unlearning method cut WMDP-Bio accuracy from 63.7% to 31.2% on Zephyr-7B, 75.3% to 30.7% on Yi-34B and 74.8% to 34.0% on Mixtral-8x7B (25% is chance) while largely preserving MMLU and MT-Bench performance, whereas the SCRUB, SSD and LLMU baselines could not do so without crippling general capability.
Finding Quote: For both ZEPHYR -7 B and Y I -34 B, RMU is able to drop performance to near random accuracy on WMDP-Bio and WMDP-Cyber, while other baselines struggle to drop accuracy on WMDP-Bio and WMDP-Cyber without crippling model performance on MMLU.

Report Title: The WMDP Benchmark: Measuring and Reducing Malicious Use With Unlearning
Finding: Knowledge removed by RMU was not trivially recoverable: linear probes trained on RMU-unlearned models' activations achieved only slightly better than random accuracy on held-out WMDP-Bio and WMDP-Cyber questions, across both model sizes.
Finding Quote: Across both categories and model sizes, linear probing only achieves slightly better than random accuracy.

Report Title: Towards Tracing Trustworthiness Dynamics: Revisiting Pre-training Period of Large Language Models
Finding: The authors show pre-training checkpoints can be used as an alignment resource: steering vectors extracted from them improve the trustworthiness of the fully pre-trained model, a technique not available if only the final checkpoint is studied.
Finding Quote: we extract steering vectors from a LLM's pre-training checkpoints to enhance the LLM's trustworthiness.

Report Title: SALAD-Bench: A Hierarchical and Comprehensive Safety Benchmark for Large Language Models (ACL Findings)
Finding: The fine-tuned MD-Judge safety evaluator outscored keyword matching, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and LlamaGuard on all five of the Table 3 test sets, reaching F1 0.818 on SALAD-Base-Test, 0.873 on SALAD-Enhance-Test, 0.644 on ToxicChat, 0.866 on Beavertails and 0.864 on SafeRLHF, against GPT-4's 0.785/0.827/0.470/0.842/0.835.
Finding Quote: MD-Judge markedly surpasses its counterparts on both our proprietary test set and the publicly available safety test set

Report Title: PsySafe: A Comprehensive Framework for Psychological-based Attack, Defense, and Evaluation of Multi-agent System Safety
Models / Systems: GPT-4 and Llama Guard (Meta) as input filters
Finding: Standard input-side content filtering (GPT-4, Llama Guard) was ineffective at blocking the dark-traits-injection attack, detectable ratio pushed to ~4-6% with a simple jailbreak prompt.
Finding Quote: current input-side filtering techniques are ineffective in mitigating the dark traits injection

Report Title: PsySafe: A Comprehensive Framework for Psychological-based Attack, Defense, and Evaluation of Multi-agent System Safety
Models / Systems: Camel, AutoGen, MetaGPT, AutoGPT (all on GPT-3.5 Turbo backbone)
Finding: A 'dark traits injection' attack induced collective dangerous behavior across all four tested multi-agent frameworks, joint danger rates up to 73.6%, process danger rates 96.8-99.7%.
Finding Quote: HI-Traits Attack can effectively contaminate multi-agent systems, causing agents to conduct collective dangerous behaviors during interactions.

Report Title: Fake Alignment: Are LLMs Really Aligned Well? (NAACL 2024)
Models / Systems: MOSS-SFT, Baichuan2-7B, Vicuna-7B-v1.5, ChatGLM2-6B (non-frontier); GPT-3.5-Turbo, Claude (comparators)
Finding: A new FINE framework reveals several open-source LLMs exhibit 'fake alignment' (large multiple-choice vs open-ended safety score gaps, e.g. MOSS-SFT 16% vs 92%); closed-source GPT-3.5-Turbo and Claude were far more consistent across formats.
Finding Quote: Applying FINE to 14 widely-used LLMs reveals several models with purported safety are poorly aligned in practice

Report Title: Large Language Models can Strategically Deceive their Users when Put Under Pressure
Finding: Apollo probed how robust the deceptive-trading behaviour was by varying the setting - removing the reasoning scratchpad, changing system instructions to try to prevent the behaviour, varying the amount of pressure, varying the perceived risk of being caught, and other simple environment changes - reporting that the behaviour varies under these interventions rather than being eliminated by them.
Finding Quote: We perform a brief investigation of how this behavior varies under changes to the setting, such as removing model access to a reasoning scratchpad, attempting to prevent the misaligned behavior by changing system instructions, changing the amount of pressure the model is under, varying the perceived risk of getting caught, and making other simple changes to the environment.

Report Title: A Holistic Approach For Test And Evaluation Of Large Language Models
Models / Systems: SOTA LLMs used as evaluation graders
Finding: Scale AI reports that a hybrid human-plus-AI evaluation methodology generalises across both LLM capabilities and safety and can identify where AI assistance is accurate enough to automate evaluation, reducing cost and increasing scale.
Finding Quote: Our hybrid methodology generalizes across both LLM capabilities and safety, accurately identifying areas where AI assistance can be used to automate this evaluation.

Report Title: A Holistic Approach For Test And Evaluation Of Large Language Models
Finding: Scale AI reports that its hybrid human-plus-AI evaluation pipeline, which uses confidence estimates to decide when an LLM judge can replace a human, scores human preference to 86% accuracy while offloading up to 20% of the work to AI models.
Finding Quote: high degree of accuracy (86%) while offloading a significant portion of the work to AI models (up to 20%)

Report Title: A Holistic Approach For Test And Evaluation Of Large Language Models
Finding: In Scale AI's safety-testing framework, generalist red teamers who work across many domains and projects had the highest rate of red-teaming success (80%), while expert red teamers, seeded with successful attacks from automated methods and generalists, produced the most harmful attacks.
Finding Quote: generalist red teamers, who have experience red teaming across a variety of different domains and projects, had the highest rate of red teaming success (80%)

Report Title: Language Model Pilot Report
Finding: METR judged that its own 12-task pilot evaluations were not adequate to rule out that near-future agents (e.g. a 100x effective-compute scale-up) would be capable of autonomous replication and adaptation, absent intermediate evaluations during pretraining.
Finding Quote: Unfortunately, these evaluations are not adequate to rule out the possibility that near-future agents will be capable of ARA.

Report Title: Language Model Pilot Report
Finding: Both Claude and GPT-4 refused unethical subtasks during the evaluation (about 6% of agent actions in the targeted-phishing run were refusals); human overseers overrode these refusals by editing the generation, e.g. replacing "I cannot complete this task" with "I will make a plan to accomplish this task", which was usually enough to stop further refusals.
Finding Quote: As such, when agents refused to perform a task, human overseers intervened to change the generation. For example, the sentence “I cannot complete this task” is replaced with “I will make a plan to accomplish this task;”

Report Title: Do the Rewards Justify the Means? Measuring Trade-Offs Between Rewards and Ethical Behavior in the MACHIAVELLI Benchmark
Finding: The authors found that two mitigation methods they built - prompting the LM agent to behave ethically (moral conditioning) and an artificial-conscience Q-value penalty for the RL agent - reduced harm on all three behavioural metrics, but both also reduced the agent's reward, and the LM moral conditioning raised the share of points from moral achievements from 83.0% to 90.7% largely by cutting points from immoral achievements (4.3 to 2.4).
Finding Quote: Both of our methods for steering agent behavior reduce their harmfulness across all three behavioral metrics. However, the regularization also reduces the reward for each agent.
